card.What will I do: Onboarding to the ISMS implementation programme. Complete onboarding: record your assignment, sign the undertaking and data rules, and submit your completed Onboarding record file.
card.Why am I doing this: Every GRC (Governance, Risk and Compliance) job starts with conduct: you handle other people's data and you produce records that auditors rely on. Before you touch any task, the organisation needs proof that you know the rules (SITL-POL-024 Section 6.1) and that your workspace records your work correctly.
What will I learn: Follow the mentee conduct and data rules — synthetic data only, own work, no AI tools for task work — see SITL-POL-024 Section 3.1; SITL-POL-022 Section 7.1
Recognise what a controlled record looks like: hash, UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) time, version, naming convention — see Capture standard — SITL-MEN-101 Section 9
Use the scripted help: the help note (?) on every step, the glossary and the "Report a problem" form — see Guided Model — principle G7
Keep task data only in your platform folders (00_Admin, 01_Inputs, 02_Working, 03_Submission) — see SITL-STD-001 Section 6 — row "Mentee use"; Capture standard — folders
card.How to do it: 6 numbered steps, of which 3 are decisions from options (judgement share 50 %). Rules you will use: copy and calculation only (Learn › Rule tables). Assigned by the Cybersecurity Program Manager, who has written the help note (?) on every step. Help is pre-written on the platform (no live chat).
What to read or refer: SITL-POL-024 — Section 3.1 policy statements; Section 6.1 Procedure: Mentee onboarding
SITL-POL-005 — Acceptable Use Policy
SITL-POL-022 — Section 7.1 Guideline: Using generative AI safely (no AI tool is used for task work)
SITL-STD-001 — Section 6 Handling matrix — row "Mentee use"
SITL Group GRC Charter — Section 10 and Section 10.1 Rules of engagement for mentees

Template: Platform forms (ADM-UND, ADM-RULES) and the file Onboarding record (ONB-RMF) (issued in /M2610-00001/W01/F1.1/01_Inputs). Submit to /M2610-00001/W01/F1.1/03_Submission. R04: Copy the first five parties listed in the table of addendum Section 4 (Stakeholder requirements), in the same order, with the requirement written next to each.
R05: Walk the SITL-STD-001 Section 5 decision tree from Q1. Then apply SITL-POL-004 Section 3.1: personal data, children's data and credentials are never below Tier 3; aggregated data takes the highest tier of its parts, and at least the tier of what the parts show when read together; derived outputs take the tier of the source.
R06: Write: "Because of <cause>, <event> may occur, leading to <consequence> for <asset>." Copy the words for cause, event and consequence from the scenario facts. Copy the asset name from the register.
R07: Find the likelihood and impact descriptor in the ERM scale table (SITL-ERM-001 Section 6.2–6.4) that uses the same words as the facts. Write the descriptor number. Residual likelihood = inherent likelihood − 1 for each existing control marked "working" (lowest value 1). Residual impact = inherent impact. Score = likelihood × impact. Rating: 1–5 Low, 6–11 Medium, 12–19 High, 20–25 Critical.
R08: LOW-criticality appetite = 11. Residual score ≤ 11 → Decision "Accept and monitor". Residual score > 11 → Decision "Treat"; due days from SITL-ERM-001 Section 7: Critical 30, High 90, Medium 180.
R10: If a sentence has two actions (joined by "and" or ";"), make two rows. Owner role = the owner of the linked SITL policy in the SITL-POL-000 index.
R15: Look up the control frequency in Ref-Sampling and copy the minimum sample. Where what you sample is a population of records (the accounts of one review), use its population-of-records row. The platform draws the sample at random once your sample size is checked.
R19: Effective: no exceptions. Effective with exceptions: only Low/Medium exceptions and ≤ 5 % of the population. Not effective: any High exception or > 5 %. Control tests (T8.2): 1–2 deviations = effective with exceptions; > 2 = not effective.
R22: One change-log row for each changed field: row ID, field, old value, new value, event ID, evidence.
R24: Class 1: on an internet-facing asset, KEV-listed or Critical → 7 days. Class 2: on an internal asset, Critical or KEV-listed → 14 days. Class 3: High → 30 days. Class 4: Medium → 90 days. Due = first detected + SLA. Exception valid only if approved by system owner AND CISO, has a compensating control, and has not expired.
R26: High = affects a Mission Critical system or no evidence exists. Medium = done late or partly. Low = record-keeping only.
R27: Use the tier from rule R35. Then include every question in Ref-Questions marked for that tier or a lower tier. Clause checklist: include every clause marked for the tier; add "transfer mechanism" if data leaves the country.
R29: Role = decided by who decides why and how the personal data is processed (SITL-POL-017 Section 3.2). DPIA required = Yes if the activity involves any of: children or students, AI/analytics/profiling, monitoring or recording, health data, identity checks (KYC/AML). Otherwise No. This is the Group's screening rule: GDPR Art.35 asks for a DPIA wherever processing is likely to result in a high risk, so an activity outside this list can still need one.
R30: For every affected office and every data-subject country, look up the regimes in addendum Section 2. Deadline = discovery time (UTC) + clock. Mark the earliest firm deadline. Tell data subjects = Yes if the data includes children's data, health data, financial data or credentials, or more than 1,000 people; otherwise No. This is the Group's screening rule: GDPR Art.34 itself asks, case by case, whether the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the people concerned. Exception (GDPR Art.34(3)(a)): No if the data was unreadable to whoever took it, for example encrypted with a key they do not have. The clocks are the controller's: where the organisation holds the data as a client's processor, it also tells that client without undue delay (GDPR Art.33(2)), early enough for the client to meet the deadline you marked.
R31: Use the 4-week template: Week 1 lesson, Week 2 poster + quiz, Week 3 phishing simulation, Week 4 results + refresher. Copy the scenario card and the 3 behaviours for your theme from Ref-Content. Approvals: HR + Legal always; add works council where addendum Section 2 lists one for the office.
R34: Answer each request with ONE evidence file: the record the auditor asks for (not a plan, a template or a policy where a record is asked for), under the same clause or control, for this office, dated inside the audit period, from a system or a controlled document (not an undated screenshot). Record its file ID and SHA-256. If no file holds what is asked, answer "No evidence available" and raise an action, with an owner and a date, to produce it from now on: never create evidence after the request.
R35: Critical: access to Tier 4 data or children's data at scale, OR a customer-facing or regulatory-critical service that is hard to replace. High: access to Tier 3 personal/confidential data at volume, OR a revenue-critical service. Medium: limited personal data or pseudonymous data, easy to replace. Low: only public/anonymous data. Check from Critical down; stop at the first match.
R36: Low → Risk owner. Medium → Org CRCO. High → Org CEO + Group CISO. Critical → Not acceptable (Board decision). Source: Charter Section 6.1. Always use this table, even if the register shows a different value.
L01: Decide each document's type from what it is for and who uses it. Requirements standard (certifiable): it sets the requirements an organisation's management system shall meet, and an accredited certification body can certify the organisation against it. Requirements for certification and audit bodies: it sets the requirements a body that audits and certifies management systems shall meet, not requirements for the organisations it certifies. Guidance standard: it gives guidance or guidelines (on controls, implementation, risk, measurement or auditing) and holds no requirements to certify against. Vocabulary: it gives the overview and the terms and definitions the family uses.
L02: Place each clause of ISO/IEC 27001 by what it does in the cycle. Plan: establishing the ISMS — understanding where it operates, who leads it, what it must achieve and what it needs. Do: operating the ISMS as planned. Check: monitoring, measuring, auditing and reviewing it. Act: correcting and improving it.
L03: Write the ISMS scope (Clause 4.3) for the office in hand, one line per part, each with the source it was read in: the organisational units, the location, the services and the technology it covers; the interested parties' requirements the ISMS addresses (CTX-IP); each exclusion with its justification, or None; and the interfaces and dependencies with activities other organisations perform, each with the Annex A control that governs it.
L04: List the ten ISMS processes (Clause 4.4), each with its owner, inputs and outputs. The owner is the role that runs the process: read it where Ref-ISMS processes (Learn › Reference pages) says, for most processes the role marked R on its row of the GRC Charter Section 16 RACI (the role abbreviations are spelled out under the table). The inputs are what the process works from; the outputs are what it hands on.
L06: A control is Applicable when a risk, a legal or contractual requirement, or a business need calls for it, and Not applicable only when the office does nothing the control governs: record that justification, and review it if that changes. Every Annex A control stays in the SoA. For an applicable control, record the source that calls for it, read in its facts: Risk, where a risk in the risk register or in your risk treatment plan (LI-RTP) is treated with it; Legal requirement, where a law or a regulator's rule requires it; Contractual requirement, where a client or supplier contract requires it (PCI DSS reaches Manila through its card-handling clients' contracts); Business need, where the Group requires it of every office or the office needs it to run. Where the facts give more than one, record the first in that order. A control is still applicable when only part of the office does what it governs.
L07: Implemented? in the SoA: for a control already sprinted, its status in your tracker T-LI-CIT (column D), with its evidence ref (column F); for a control whose sprint is still to come, Planned, with its sprint and week; for an excluded control, Not applicable. The platform carries them over from the tracker and the plan.
L08: Check the information security policy against Clause 5.2 a)–g), one item at a time. Found only when you can cite the section of the policy that meets the item: the section whose own words say it. Where a statement points on to another section (a procedure, the document control), cite the statement. What an office reports doing counts only where the policy or its record shows it. Gap: no section meets the item, and its section is None.

The days are SITL-POL-010 Section 4's for a LOW organisation, as SITL-ADD-16 Section 5 sets them for GlobalConnect.
Due = first detected + the class's days, counted in calendar days from the date the finding was first detected (SITL-POL-010 Section 3.1 and Section 6.1, step 2).

Within SLA: closed on or before its due date and verified by a later scan that no longer finds it; open, with its due date not yet passed; or past its due date under a valid exception. Anything else is a breach: closed after its due date, or open past its due date with no valid exception. A closure that no later scan confirms, or that a later scan still finds, is open again with its original due date (SITL-POL-010 Section 6.1, step 4, and Section 10).

Approved by the system owner and the CISO, with a compensating control recorded, and not expired on the date it is relied on; it lasts six months at most. A compensating control reduces the risk but never closes the finding (SITL-POL-010 Section 7.1).
For each class: findings within SLA ÷ all findings of the class × 100, to one decimal. Targets: classes 1–2, 90% or more (red below 80%); classes 3–4, 95% or more (SITL-POL-010 Section 10).

Ref-Certification card.note: How ISO/IEC 27001 certification runs, summarised in our own words from ISO/IEC 17021-1 (requirements for bodies that audit and certify management systems) and ISO/IEC 27006-1 (its additional requirements for information security management systems). The auditor reviews the ISMS's documented information and the organisation's readiness for Stage 2: the scope, the information security policy, the risk assessment and treatment process, the Statement of Applicability, and whether internal audits and management reviews are planned and performed. It ends with documented conclusions, including any area of concern that could be graded a nonconformity at Stage 2.

The auditor evaluates on site whether the ISMS is implemented and effective: interviews, records and observation, with samples of the Statement of Applicability's controls in operation. Findings are graded major or minor nonconformities, and the lead auditor recommends whether to certify.

Minor: the certification body reviews and accepts the organisation's plan for correction and corrective action before it decides. Major: it reviews and accepts the correction and the corrective action and verifies that they are effective before it certifies. Some bodies already grade Stage 1 findings as minor or major.
Made by the certification body after Stage 2, by people who did not carry out the audit. The auditor does not issue the certificate.

The certificate is valid for three years. Surveillance audits come at least once a calendar year, the first no later than 12 months after the certification decision: in practice in years two and three. Each covers part of the ISMS, with the internal audits, management reviews, complaints and the actions on earlier nonconformities.
Before the certificate expires at the end of year three, a recertification audit of the whole ISMS; a positive decision starts a new three-year cycle.

Ref-Maturity Model.note: The maturity scale of the GRC Charter Section 3.3 (CMMI-style), Levels 1 to 4, used here to rate how one office practises a clause or a control, from what was found. Ask its questions in order and stop at the first No. 1) Is there a documented, approved way of doing it, and records that it is done? No → Level 1. 2) Is it the Group's standard way, done the same in every office, and reviewed at least once a year? No → Level 2. 3) Is it measured against targets, with the results tracked and acted on? No → Level 3; Yes → Level 4. The Charter puts every Group organisation at Level 3, Defined, and aims for Level 4, Quantitatively Managed, then Level 5, Optimizing: that rates the Group's GRC processes (the Charter, the Group Policy Library, the common control framework), which every organisation has adopted. An office's own practice of one clause can sit below it: where the office still does a requirement its own way, without records, or not at all, that clause rates Level 1 or 2 even though the Group stands at Level 3. Level 5 is the Group's aim for its programme as a whole and is not used to rate one clause. Status (rule L13) and level are separate questions: the level rates how what is in place is done.

LI-A.5.3.note: LI-A.5.3 · Segregation of duties. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.3; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.3. Owner role: Compliance Manager. What it requires: 1) The duties that conflict are identified: for example, requesting and approving the same thing, or creating a record and approving the payment it leads to. 2) Conflicting duties are given to different people, so that no one person can misuse an asset or let an error pass unnoticed. 3) Where duties cannot be split, for example in a small team, a compensating control is put in place, such as an independent review or monitoring, with an owner. Evidence focus: A list of the conflicting duties at the office, how each is kept apart, and the compensating control where it is not. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

Role assignments or approval settings showing the duties held by different people

The compensating control, its owner and the records of its reviews

LI-A.5.4.note: LI-A.5.4 · Management responsibilities. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.4; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.4. Owner role: Org CEO. What it requires: 1) Managers know and accept their own security duties, and support the policy. 2) Before people are given access to information and systems, their manager briefs them on their security role and responsibilities. 3) Managers require their people to apply security as the policies and procedures say, and to complete the security training their role needs. Evidence focus: Records that managers accepted their security duties and brief their people before access is given. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

How would you measure it at Level 4?

Who owns it at the office?

Is it done the Group's way, in every office, and reviewed each year?

The evidence item each sub-task produces, kept as a file in 02_Working.

What is missing, and what is the next action?
The gap and the next action, written in column G of the tracker.

LI-A.5.9.note: LI-A.5.9 · Inventory of information and other associated assets. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.9; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.9. Owner role: Chief Information Officer (CIO). What it requires: 1) An inventory of the office's information and other associated assets (systems, services, equipment) is drawn up and kept accurate and up to date. 2) Every asset in the inventory has an owner, who answers for it. 3) The inventory is reviewed at planned intervals and checked against what is actually in use, so that assets missing from it are found. Evidence focus: An inventory of the office's assets, each with its owner, that is reviewed and reconciled with what is really in use. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.12.note: LI-A.5.12 · Classification of information. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.12; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.12. Owner role: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). What it requires: 1) A classification scheme is set, based on the confidentiality, integrity and availability the information needs and on interested parties' requirements. 2) Each information asset is classified by its owner, by the scheme, and the classification is recorded in the inventory. 3) Classifications are reviewed, and changed when the information, its use or its legal context changes. Evidence focus: The scheme in use, each asset's classification decided by it and recorded, and reviews that keep them current. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.8.note: LI-A.5.8 · Information security in project management. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.8; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.8. Owner role: Cybersecurity Program Manager. What it requires: 1) Information security is built into the office's project method, whatever the type of project. 2) Each project's information security risks are assessed and treated at its start, and reviewed at each stage until it closes. 3) Security requirements are set for what each project delivers, and responsibility for security in the project is assigned. Evidence focus: Records that each project of the year was run with security in its method: its risks assessed at the start and at each gate, and its security requirements and owner set. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

RV-Q fixed questions.note: The eight questions a reviewer asks of every RV card of the Review Deck, and where each answer is found. RV-Q1 to RV-Q5 give the level, RV-Q6 the ISO reference, RV-Q7 the grade of a nonconformity, RV-Q8 the gap and the recommendation.
r: Is there a documented, approved way of doing it?
The card's scenario. No → Level 1 (the Maturity Model's first question, Ref-Maturity Model).
Are there records that it is done?
The card's scenario: logs, signed records, minutes. None → Level 1.
Is it the Group's standard way, done the same in every office?
The card's scenario: "the Group's", "every office", or the office's own way. Its own → Level 2.
Is it reviewed at least once a year?
The card's scenario. Never reviewed → Level 2.
Is it measured against targets, with the results acted on?
The card's scenario. Not measured → Level 3; measured → Level 4.

Ref-Review references (Learn › Reference pages): what each clause and control you can choose requires.
In the period or the sample, was it never done, or did more than half fail?
The card's numbers, against rule L17 (Learn › Rule tables): yes → Major; any other failure → Minor.
What is missing, and what is the next action that takes it a level up?
The first question the card answers No; the next action is what would turn it to Yes, with its owner.

LI-A.5.10.note: LI-A.5.10 · Acceptable use of information and other associated assets. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.10; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.10. Owner role: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). What it requires: 1) Rules for the acceptable use of information and other associated assets are documented. 2) Everyone who uses them, staff and external users such as contractors, is made aware of the rules and accepts them. 3) Procedures for handling information by its classification are in place and followed. Evidence focus: The acceptable-use rules in force, and a record that every user, staff and contractors, has accepted them. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. LI-A.5.11.note: LI-A.5.11 · Return of assets. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.11; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.11. Owner role: HR & Workforce Management lead. What it requires: 1) Everyone who leaves, or whose role or contract changes, returns the organisation's assets they hold (equipment, access cards, documents) by their last day. 2) Each return is checked against the assets issued to the person, and recorded. 3) Where a leaver holds knowledge that ongoing work depends on, it is written down and handed over before they go. Evidence focus: Records that each leaver returned what was issued to them, checked against the issue record, with a handover where needed. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.13.note: LI-A.5.13 · Labelling of information. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.13; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.13. Owner role: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). What it requires: 1) A labelling procedure, following the classification scheme, covers information in every format: documents, e-mail, systems, paper and media. 2) Information is labelled as the procedure says, with visible labels or metadata, and the procedure says where a label may be left off. 3) The people who handle the information know the procedure and how to apply the labels. Evidence focus: A labelling procedure for every format, labels that are actually applied, and people who know how. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.14.note: LI-A.5.14 · Information transfer. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.14; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.14. Owner role: Security Architecture & Standards Manager. What it requires: 1) Rules or procedures are set for every way information is transferred: electronic (e-mail, file transfer), physical media and verbal. 2) Transfers with external parties are covered by agreements that say how the information is protected. 3) Transfers follow the rules: information leaves only through approved, protected channels. Evidence focus: The transfers the office makes with other parties, each with its rule or agreement, and proof the rules are followed. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.6.3.note: LI-A.6.3 · Information security awareness, education and training. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 6.3; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 6.3. Owner role: Security Awareness & Training Specialist. What it requires: 1) An awareness, education and training programme is set up in line with the information security policy and the topic-specific policies, and planned so that it is repeated, not given once. 2) Everyone who works for the office receives awareness training suited to their job: at induction, and regularly after it, including when the policies change. 3) The programme's effect is checked: what people learnt is tested, for example by a quiz or a phishing simulation, and the results are recorded and acted on. Evidence focus: Records that everyone at the office is trained at induction and every year, from a planned programme, and that what they learnt is checked. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.7.note: LI-A.5.7 · Threat intelligence. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.7; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.7. Owner role: Cyber Threat Intelligence Analyst. What it requires: 1) Information about threats is collected from identified, vetted sources, inside and outside the organisation, and analysed for what it means for the office's assets. 2) The threat intelligence that results is relevant, in context and actionable, and it reaches the people who must act on it. 3) It is used: it feeds the risk assessment, and the choice and testing of controls. Evidence focus: Records of where threat information comes from, the briefs that analyse it for the office, and the risks and controls it changed. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.6.1.note: LI-A.6.1 · Screening. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 6.1; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 6.1. Owner role: HR & Workforce Management lead. What it requires: 1) Everyone who is to join is screened before they start: employees, and contractors and temporary staff too, including those placed by an agency, whose contract with the agency requires the screening. 2) The checks are proportionate to the role: to the information it will access, the risks and the law (at Manila, the Data Privacy Act of 2012), and each result is recorded. 3) Where screening cannot be completed before someone starts, the exception is recorded and their access is restricted until it is complete. Evidence focus: The checks each role needs, the screening records of the year's starters, and how a start before screening is complete is handled. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.6.7.note: LI-A.6.7 · Remote working. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 6.7; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 6.7. Owner role: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). What it requires: 1) Rules for remote working are set and approved: who may work remotely, from where, on which equipment, and how information is protected there. 2) Security measures protect information accessed, processed or stored outside the office: protected devices, and a secure connection with multi-factor authentication. 3) Remote workers are told the rules and acknowledge them before they start working remotely. Evidence focus: The office's remote working rules, the measures that protect remote workers' devices and connections, and how the risks of remote access are treated. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.19.note: LI-A.5.19 · Information security in supplier relationships. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.19; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.19. Owner role: Vendor / Third-Party Risk Analyst. What it requires: 1) A documented process manages the information security risks of using suppliers' products and services: each supplier is identified and recorded with its type and the risk it brings (its tier). 2) Each supplier is assessed before it is engaged and before information is shared with it, and the security requirements for it are set from that assessment. 3) Each supplier relationship is managed through its life to its end: when it ends, the supplier's access is removed and the information is returned and deleted. Evidence focus: A supplier register with each supplier's tier, assessments dated before each contract, and records of how a supplier relationship is ended. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.23.note: LI-A.5.23 · Information security for use of cloud services. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.23; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.23. Owner role: Security Architecture & Standards Manager. What it requires: 1) Each cloud service is acquired through the approval process, with a security assessment before it is used (SITL-POL-021 Section 6.1). 2) The responsibilities shared between the cloud provider and the office are recorded for each service, and the office runs its own share: access, its data and its configuration. 3) The service's use and exit are managed: it is recorded in the cloud service register, monitored, and has an exit plan for its data. Evidence focus: For each cloud service: its approval, its shared-responsibility matrix, and how its data would be got back at exit. LI-A.5.30.note: LI-A.5.30 · ICT readiness for business continuity. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.30; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.30. Owner role: Business Continuity & Resilience Analyst. LI-A.5.31.note: LI-A.5.31 · Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.31; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.31. LI-A.5.37.note: LI-A.5.37 · Documented operating procedures. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.37; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.37. Owner role: Chief Information Officer (CIO). What it requires: 1) Operating procedures are documented for the office's IT operating activities, for example backup and restore, start-up and shutdown, and monitoring. 2) The procedures are available to the people who need them, where they do the work. 3) Each procedure is under document control: identified, approved by management, reviewed and updated when needed, and every change authorised. LI-A.6.5.note: LI-A.6.5 · Responsibilities after termination or change of employment. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 6.5; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 6.5. Owner role: HR & Workforce Management lead. What it requires: 1) The information security responsibilities that stay valid after someone leaves or changes role are defined: keeping information confidential, intellectual property, and what any confidentiality agreement says. 2) They are told to the person when they leave or change role, and the person acknowledges them. 3) A change of role is handled as the end of the old responsibilities and the start of the new, and the people who need to know are told. What it requires: 1) Managers regularly review that information processing in their area complies with the security policies, rules and standards. 2) Where non-compliance is found, its cause is found, corrective action is taken, and the action is checked. 3) The results of the reviews and the actions are recorded and reported. Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).
r: Show the managers' compliance reviews: each review's area, date and result.
Show the cause found and the corrective action taken for each non-compliance.

Show the review results reported to management.

LI-A.5.15.note: LI-A.5.15 · Access control. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.15; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.15. Owner role: Security Architecture & Standards Manager. What it requires: 1) A topic-specific policy on access control is set and approved: access is given on need-to-know and least privilege, with the asset owner's approval. 2) Access rules are set for each system: which role gets which access, and who approves it, from the business and security needs of the information it holds. 3) The rules are applied: what each role holds matches its rule, and the rules are reviewed when a system, a role or a process changes. Evidence focus: The access control policy in force at the office, and each system's access rules by role, with what each role holds held against them. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).
r: Set the access rules of each system: which role gets which access, on what need, and who approves it.
The access rules matrix by system and role

The account extract compared with the access rules, and the removal record

LI-A.8.8.note: LI-A.8.8 · Management of technical vulnerabilities. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.8; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.8. Owner role: Vulnerability Management Governance Analyst. What it requires: 1) Every asset in scope is scanned for technical vulnerabilities, as often as SITL-POL-010 Section 3.1 sets. 2) Each finding is classified by exposure and exploitation, and fixed by its due date (SITL-POL-010 Section 4) or covered by a valid exception. 3) Each fix is verified by a later scan, and remediation is reported against the timescales each month. Evidence focus: Records that findings are found, dated, fixed on time and verified, and that SLA compliance is measured. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).
r: Show that findings are classified and dated against the timescales, tested on a sample.
An SLA test of a sample of findings: class, due date and status of each (rule R24)

The monthly SLA reports, with the closures verified by re-scan

LI-A.8.13.note: LI-A.8.13 · Information backup. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.13; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.13. Owner role: Chief Information Officer (CIO). What it requires: 1) Backup copies of information, software and systems are kept, as the topic-specific policy on backup says. 2) They are tested regularly by restoring them. 3) The backup procedure is approved and the backups are logged. Evidence focus: Records that the backups run, can be restored, and are taken as often as each service needs. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.17.note: LI-A.5.17 · Authentication information. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.17; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.17. Owner role: Security Architecture & Standards Manager. What it requires: 1) Authentication information, such as a first password, is issued securely to the right person and changed at first use. 2) People are told to keep their authentication information secret, never to share it, and to report it if it is disclosed, and they accept those rules. 3) Systems enforce the policy's sign-in rules: strong passwords, and multi-factor authentication for remote, privileged and Tier 3/4 access (SITL-POL-006 Section 3.1). Evidence focus: How first passwords are issued and changed, the users' acceptance of the rules, and each system's sign-in settings. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.32.note: LI-A.5.32 · Intellectual property rights. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.32; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.32. Owner role: Compliance Manager. What it requires: 1) Rules for using software and other material protected by intellectual property (licences, copyright) are set and known to staff. 2) Software is acquired from known sources, and licence records are kept, with installations kept within the licences held. 3) Compliance with the licences is checked, and a shortfall is put right. Evidence focus: The licence records against what is installed, and the rule staff follow. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

Licence compliance check and its actions

LI-A.5.33.note: LI-A.5.33 · Protection of records. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.33; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.33. Owner role: Compliance Manager. What it requires: 1) The office's records are identified, each with the retention period that law, contracts and the business require. 2) Records are protected from loss, destruction, falsification and unauthorised access or release for as long as they are kept. 3) Records are disposed of at the end of their retention period, and the disposal is recorded. Evidence focus: A retention schedule for the office's records, and proof that records are protected and disposed of on time. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.34.note: LI-A.5.34 · Privacy and protection of personal identifiable information (PII). ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.34; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.34. Owner role: Data Protection Officer (DPO). What it requires: 1) The privacy and PII protection requirements that apply (laws, regulations, contracts) are identified, and a privacy policy is communicated. 2) Each processing activity is recorded with its lawful basis, and screened for a DPIA before it starts. 3) Someone is responsible for privacy (a DPO), and the measures that protect PII are in place. Evidence focus: The record of processing activities with lawful bases and DPIA screenings, and the DPO's appointment. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.35.note: LI-A.5.35 · Independent review of information security. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.35; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.35. Owner role: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). What it requires: 1) The office's way of managing information security is reviewed independently, at planned intervals and when significant changes occur. 2) Reviewers are independent of the area they review (internal audit, an independent manager or an external party) and competent to review it. 3) The results are reported to the management that asked for the review, and the corrective actions are tracked. Evidence focus: A plan of independent reviews, the reviewers' independence, and the reports and actions that follow. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.20.note: LI-A.5.20 · Addressing information security within supplier agreements. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.20; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.20. Owner role: Vendor / Third-Party Risk Analyst. What it requires: 1) The security requirements for each supplier are set from the type of relationship and its risk (its tier), in a clause checklist. 2) The requirements are written into the agreement: for example confidentiality, security obligations, incident notification, audit, sub-contracting, return and deletion of information, termination and transfers. 3) Each agreement is checked against the checklist before it is signed, and every missing or short clause is negotiated or recorded with its decision. Evidence focus: Each supplier agreement held against the clause checklist for its tier, the clauses in the signed agreement, and a record of how each gap was dealt with. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.5.22.note: LI-A.5.22 · Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.22; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.22. Owner role: Vendor / Third-Party Risk Analyst. What it requires: 1) Each supplier's service and its information security are monitored and reviewed at planned intervals, more often for a higher tier. 2) The incidents and service reports a supplier sends are reviewed and followed up. 3) A change to a supplier's service (a new sub-processor, location or version) is assessed before it takes effect, and the supplier is reassessed when its tier says. Evidence focus: Supplier reviews held on a schedule set by tier, with incidents and changes assessed and followed up. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.7.3.note: LI-A.7.3 · Securing offices, rooms and facilities. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.3; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.3. Owner role: Manila facilities manager. What it requires: 1) Rooms that hold sensitive information or equipment are sited away from public access, and locked. 2) They give no sign of what is inside: no sign naming the server room, nothing sensitive visible from outside. 3) Directories and plans that show where the sensitive rooms are are not available to the public. Evidence focus: A list of the sensitive rooms with how each is locked, and proof that nothing outside points to them. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.7.4.note: LI-A.7.4 · Physical security monitoring. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.4; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.4. Owner role: Manila facilities manager. What it requires: 1) The premises are monitored all the time for unauthorised physical access, for example by CCTV, intruder alarms or guards. 2) The monitoring covers every entry point and secure area; recordings are kept for a set period, and only named people may view them. 3) The monitoring is tested regularly, and its alarms are responded to. Evidence focus: The camera and alarm layout against the entry points and secure areas, and records of tests and responses. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.7.5.note: LI-A.7.5 · Protecting against physical and environmental threats. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.5; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.5. Owner role: Manila facilities manager. What it requires: 1) The physical and environmental threats to the site are assessed: fire, flood and water, earthquake, storm, power loss and the like. 2) Equipment rooms are protected against them: fire detection and suppression, water detection, and not sited below or beside a water source without protection. 3) The protections are inspected and tested. Evidence focus: The site threat assessment, and records that the protections it calls for are in place and tested. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? LI-A.7.6.note: LI-A.7.6 · Working in secure areas. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.6; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.6. Owner role: Manila facilities manager. What it requires: 1) Rules for working in the secure areas are set and made known to everyone who enters them. 2) Work by contractors and visitors in a secure area is supervised, and vacant secure areas are locked and checked. 3) Photography, video and sound recording are not allowed in a secure area unless authorised. Evidence focus: The rules for the secure areas, and records that visits are supervised and the rooms checked. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? LI-A.7.7.note: LI-A.7.7 · Clear desk and clear screen. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.7; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.7. Owner role: Org CISO. What it requires: 1) Papers and removable media with sensitive information are locked away when not in use, above all outside working hours. 2) Screens are locked, and devices logged off, when the user is away. 3) Printouts are collected at once, for example by secure print release, and whiteboards and flip charts are wiped after use. Evidence focus: The clear desk and clear screen rule, the screen-lock setting, and records of the desk checks. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? LI-A.7.8.note: LI-A.7.8 · Equipment siting and protection. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.8; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.8. Owner role: Head of Infrastructure. What it requires: 1) Equipment is sited where it is safe from unauthorised access and from physical and environmental threats. 2) Screens and devices that show sensitive information are placed so that people who are not authorised cannot see them. 3) Equipment is protected: racks and cabinets are locked, and no eating, drinking or smoking is allowed near it. Evidence focus: Where the equipment that handles client data is sited, and how it is protected. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? LI-A.7.9.note: LI-A.7.9 · Security of assets off-premises. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.9; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.9. Owner role: Chief Information Officer. What it requires: 1) Devices taken off the premises, such as laptops for home working, are authorised and recorded against their holder. 2) They are protected off site: encrypted, and never left unattended in a public place or a car. 3) The record of who holds which device off site is kept up to date. Evidence focus: The register of devices off site, with holder, approval and encryption. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? LI-A.7.10.note: LI-A.7.10 · Storage media. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.10; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.10. Owner role: Chief Information Officer. What it requires: 1) Removable storage media are managed through their life: issued, recorded and encrypted as the handling matrix requires for the information's tier. 2) Media are stored securely when not in use, and removable storage is allowed only where it is needed. 3) Media no longer needed are disposed of securely. Evidence focus: The register of removable media, and proof that removable storage is blocked where it is not approved. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.7.11.note: LI-A.7.11 · Supporting utilities. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.11; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.11. Owner role: Head of Infrastructure. What it requires: 1) The utilities the equipment depends on (power, telecoms, cooling) meet its needs, and the office knows which ones it depends on. 2) A UPS and a generator keep critical equipment running through a power cut. 3) The utilities and their backups are inspected and tested regularly, and alarm on failure. Evidence focus: The utilities the office depends on, their backups, and records of their tests. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? LI-A.7.12.note: LI-A.7.12 · Cabling security. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.12; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.12. Owner role: Head of Infrastructure. What it requires: 1) Power and network cables are protected from interception, interference and damage, for example in conduits or trays. 2) Power cables are kept apart from network cables, and cables are labelled. 3) Patch panels and cable rooms are locked, in secure areas or cabinets, and the cable routes are documented. Evidence focus: The cable routes, and proof that patch panels are locked and cables kept apart and labelled. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? LI-A.7.13.note: LI-A.7.13 · Equipment maintenance. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 7.13; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 7.13. Owner role: Head of Infrastructure. What it requires: 1) Equipment is maintained at the intervals its supplier recommends. 2) Only authorised people maintain it, and every service and fault is recorded. 3) Equipment sent away for repair is first cleared of sensitive information, or the repair is supervised. LI-A.5.5.note: LI-A.5.5 · Contact with authorities. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.5; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.5. Owner role: Data Protection Officer (DPO). What it requires: 1) The authorities the office may need to contact are identified, such as the data protection authority, regulators and law enforcement, with when and by whom each is contacted. 2) Their contact details, and the people who contact them, are kept current. 3) Incidents and other matters an authority must be told of are reported to it in time, and each contact is recorded. Owner role: Incident Response & Crisis Manager (GRC). What it requires: 1) A way to report observed or suspected security events is set, easy to reach and always available. 2) All personnel know it, and know that they must report promptly. 3) Each report is logged when received and passed on to be assessed. What it requires: 1) Secure coding rules are set and applied before, during and after coding: a coding standard, peer review and approved tools. 2) Code is reviewed and scanned for vulnerabilities before release, and each finding is fixed or accepted with a recorded reason and approval. 3) Developers are trained in secure coding, and the open-source and third-party components used are tracked and kept up to date. LI-A.8.32.note: LI-A.8.32 · Change management. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.32; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.32. Owner role: Chief Information Officer. What it requires: 1) Changes to systems follow a change procedure: each is recorded, its impact assessed, and it is approved before it is made. 2) Each change is tested, has a rollback plan and is reviewed after it is made; an emergency change follows a documented emergency path and is approved and reviewed retrospectively. 3) Change records are kept and checked, so that a change made outside the procedure is found. What it requires: 1) A scheme for categorising and prioritising events is agreed, with the criteria for each level. 2) Each reported event is assessed against it by a named point of contact, who decides whether it is an incident. 3) Each assessment and decision is recorded, with its reason. LI-A.5.26.note: LI-A.5.26 · Response to information security incidents. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.26; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.26. Owner role: Incident Response & Crisis Manager (GRC). What it requires: 1) Incidents are responded to by the people designated, following documented procedures. 2) The response contains the incident, escalates it where the procedure says, and tells the parties who must know, the authorities among them. 3) The response is logged, and each incident is formally closed once recovered. Evidence focus: Records that each incident was contained, escalated and communicated as the procedure says, and closed. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. LI-A.5.27.note: LI-A.5.27 · Learning from information security incidents. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.27; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.27. Owner role: Incident Response & Crisis Manager (GRC). What it requires: 1) After an incident, a review establishes its root cause and the lessons. 2) The lessons become actions on controls, procedures, the risk assessment or training, each with an owner and a date, and are followed to closure. 3) Incidents are counted by type, volume and cost, to find those that recur or do the most harm. Evidence focus: Records that each review's lessons became tracked actions, and that incidents are analysed for patterns. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.8.1.note: LI-A.8.1 · User endpoint devices. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.1; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.1. Owner role: Security Architecture & Standards Manager. What it requires: 1) A topic-specific policy on user endpoint devices sets how they are registered, configured and handled, on and off the premises. 2) Each device is registered and built to a secure configuration: storage encrypted, screen locked when idle, software installation restricted. 3) Users know their responsibilities for their devices, and a lost or stolen device can be dealt with, for example wiped remotely. Evidence focus: Records that every endpoint at the office is known, built securely and in the hands of users who know their duties. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? Ask the fixed questions LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (LI-Q fixed questions).

LI-A.8.16.note: LI-A.8.16 · Monitoring activities. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.16; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.16. Owner role: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). What it requires: 1) Networks, systems and applications are monitored for anomalous behaviour, with alert rules set from what is normal. 2) Monitoring covers what the policy sets: every Mission Critical and internet-facing system at Manila (SITL-ADD-16 Section 5). 3) Alerts are reviewed and acted on in time, with the cover the policy sets: business hours and on-call alerting at Manila. Evidence focus: Records that the right systems are watched, and that alerts reach someone who acts on them, at any hour. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. LI-A.8.17.note: LI-A.8.17 · Clock synchronization. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.17; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.17. Owner role: Chief Information Officer (CIO). What it requires: 1) The clocks of all systems are synchronised to approved reference time sources. 2) The time sources and how systems use them are documented. 3) Clock drift is detected, so that events from different systems line up. Evidence focus: Records that every system keeps the same time, so logs can be lined up as evidence. Each sub-task below produces one evidence item; sub-task 01 is the first. Unsure? LI-A.8.25.note: LI-A.8.25 · Secure development life cycle. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.25; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.25. Owner role: Security Architecture & Standards Manager. What it requires: 1) Rules for developing software and systems securely are set and applied in every phase of the life cycle, from requirements to release. 2) Security checkpoints (gates) are set in the life cycle, and the development environments, source code repositories and pipeline are protected. 3) Each release passes its security checkpoints, and the result is recorded. Evidence focus: A record of the life cycle the office's developers follow, with the security activity and gate at each stage, and proof that releases passed them. LI-A.8.33.note: LI-A.8.33 · Test information. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.33; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.33. Owner role: Data Protection Officer (DPO). What it requires: 1) Test information is chosen with care: production personal or confidential data is not used for testing or, where it must be, it is masked or removed first. 2) Each copy of production data into a test environment is authorised, protected with the same access controls as production, and logged. 3) Test information is deleted from the test environment once the testing is finished. Evidence focus: A log of every copy of production data into test, with who authorised it, whether it was masked and when it was deleted. LI-A.8.34.note: LI-A.8.34 · Protection of information systems during audit testing. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.34; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.34. Owner role: Information Security Auditor. What it requires: 1) Audit tests on operational systems are planned and agreed with the system's management beforehand: scope, timing and who tests. 2) Testers get read-only access where possible; anything more is run by experienced people, outside business hours where it could affect availability, and watched. 3) Access given for a test is logged and removed when the test ends. Evidence focus: The signed scope of each audit test on live systems, and the records that test access was read-only, watched and removed. What it requires: 1) Privileged access is granted through an approval, only to those who need it, for what they need it for. 2) Privileged activities use accounts separate from everyday ones, with strong authentication. 3) Privileged rights are reviewed at set intervals (quarterly at Manila, SITL-ADD-16 Section 5), and their use is recorded. Owner role: Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). What it requires: 1) Access to information and to application functions is restricted by role, as the access control policy sets. 2) Each system gives a user only the information their role needs. 3) No shared store opens Tier 3 or Tier 4 information to people whose role does not need it. What it requires: 1) Read and write access to source code, development tools and software libraries is restricted to those who need it. 2) Write access is given on approval, and changes to the code go through the repository. 3) Access to the code, and every change to it, is logged. What it requires: 1) Users and systems authenticate with the strength the information needs: multi-factor for remote, privileged and Tier 3 or Tier 4 access. 2) Log-on limits failed attempts and protects passwords in transit and in storage. 3) Idle sessions are closed, and log-on attempts are recorded. LI-A.8.6.note: LI-A.8.6 · Capacity management. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.6; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.6. Owner role: Chief Information Officer (CIO). What it requires: 1) The use of systems, networks and facilities is monitored. 2) Future capacity needs are projected from what the business plans, and planned for. 3) Capacity is added before a limit is reached, so that the service keeps its agreed levels. What it requires: 1) Logs of user activity, exceptions, faults and security events are produced by the systems that need them. 2) Logs are protected from change and deletion, including by the systems' own administrators. 3) Logs are kept as long as the policy sets: 12 months for security event logs (SITL-POL-009 Section 3.4). LI-A.8.26.note: LI-A.8.26 · Application security requirements. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.26; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 8.26. Owner role: Security Architecture & Standards Manager. What it requires: 1) Security requirements are identified and specified when an application is developed or acquired, from the information it handles, its risks and the legal and contractual requirements on it. 2) An application that handles transactions or payments has requirements that protect them: complete, not altered, not repeated, and kept confidential. 3) The requirements are approved, and tested before the application or the change goes live. What it requires: 1) Principles for engineering secure systems are set and documented, for example security designed into each layer, least privilege and defence in depth. 2) Every new system and every significant design change is reviewed against the principles before it is built. 3) The principles are reviewed regularly and kept up to date. Owner role: Vulnerability Management Governance Analyst. What it requires: 1) Security testing is planned and run during development, for every release: tests of the security functions and scans for vulnerabilities. 2) New and changed systems pass an acceptance test, security included, against set criteria before they go live. 3) Independent tests, such as a penetration test, are run as policy requires, and their findings acted on. Owner role: Security Architecture & Standards Manager. What it requires: 1) Development, test and production environments are kept separate, each on its own systems or accounts. 2) Changes reach production only through the approved release path; developers have no standing access to change production systems or data. 3) Anyone who works in more than one environment uses separate accounts there, and development tools are not reachable from production. h: What was found at the Manila office
r: 4.1 Understanding the organization and its context

The issues are recorded in CTX-ISS on the Group template T-LI-CTX, the way every GlobalConnect office records them, climate change included. The Compliance Manager reviews the list every six months, and the record of each review is kept.
4.2 Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties

The interested parties are recorded in CTX-IP, copied from the Group table in SITL-ADD-16 Section 4. The client contracts and data-protection agreements, which hold most of Manila's requirements, have not been read into it. The Manila team keeps the register its own way, and it has never been reviewed.
4.3 Determining the scope of the information security management system

A scope statement for Manila is drafted in LI-SCOPE: units, location, services, technology, interfaces and exclusions. It is a draft: neither the Org CEO nor the Group CISO has approved it, and nothing yet records it as the ISMS's scope.

Manila runs seven of the ten ISMS processes of the Group's process model, with records. Internal audit, management review and corrective action have never run there. Nobody has reviewed the set of processes at Manila.

The Org CEO approved SITL-ADD-16 with the Group CISO, effective 1 October 2026, and signs a yearly ISMS commitment statement, as every Group organisation's CEO does. The ISMS budget is in the approved plan, and the minutes of the CEO's quarterly security briefings to Manila managers are kept. The Group reviews the commitment each year.

SITL-POL-001, the Group information security policy, applies at Manila through SITL-ADD-16, the same policy in every office. It is approved by the Group GRC Steering Committee and kept under document control, with a yearly review. Two things the clause asks for are missing: nothing records that it was communicated to the workforce (its document control shows no communication record attached), and it is classified Internal, with no way set for clients or other interested parties to obtain it. Nobody measures how well staff know it.

The GRC Charter Section 16 sets the Group's roles, but at Manila day-to-day ownership of the ISMS is not assigned to any role, and the Manila job descriptions say nothing about security responsibilities. No record shows the roles were communicated at Manila.
6.1.1 Actions to address risks and opportunities: general

Manila's own risk-planning sheet turns the issues of CTX-ISS and the requirements of CTX-IP into risks, approved by the Org CISO. It records no opportunities and no way of evaluating whether the actions worked. It has not been reviewed since it was written.
Risk assessments use the Group method in every office and are reviewed each year; no measures or targets.

A risk treatment plan for Manila names an owner and a date for each risk, and the risk owners' approval is recorded. The Statement of Applicability is the Group's generic one, not yet worked out from Manila's own risks. The plan is Manila's own sheet and has not been reviewed.
6.2 Information security objectives and planning to achieve them

Manila's four information security objectives for 2026 were set from the risk assessment and approved by the Org CEO with targets, owners and dates, by the Group procedure in SITL-POL-001 Section 6.2, as in every organisation. Progress is measured each quarter on the objectives dashboard against the Group's target of 80% on track, and an objective that falls behind gets a corrective plan: two did in the second quarter. The objectives themselves are reviewed each year.

Changes to the ISMS are made as they come, decided by whoever asks for them, with no documented way of planning them and no record of most. Only one change, the SIEM's move to a hybrid set-up, was planned with a written impact note.

The ISMS's resources for Manila (the CISO office, three GRC analysts, tools and a training budget) are approved in the Group's yearly budget cycle, the same way for every organisation, and the needs are reviewed each year. Nothing is measured against a target.

Manila keeps its own list of the skills each security role needs, approved by the Org CISO, and records of the training each person attended. Nobody checks whether the training made people competent, and the list has never been reviewed.

New agents get security awareness training once, at induction, from Manila's own slide deck, with attendance recorded; there is no refresher. In a spot check, four of ten agents could not say where to report a suspicious call. The deck has never been reviewed.

What to communicate about the ISMS, when, to whom and how is set in the Group communication plan, which every office follows. Manila sends the monthly security bulletin and the quarterly client updates, with records, and the plan is reviewed each year.

The ISMS documents sampled in the Group library follow the Group document-control procedure (SITL-POL-000 Section 7): each has an ID, version, approver and review date. Retention and disposal are reviewed each year. The Manila IT team also keeps its own operating procedures on the office wiki, outside the library: the pages the analysis opened carry no version, owner or approval date.

The Group procedures say how the ISMS processes are run, but Manila keeps no record that they were carried out as planned. The payroll that the outside provider runs is not controlled: nobody checks the provider's work against the agreement.

The Manila risk assessment was performed in March 2026 on the Group method, the same way as in every office, with the results in the risk register and the next yearly run booked for March 2027. It was not performed again when the office took on healthcare-claims clients in August 2026, a significant change, so no health-data risks are on the register.
Manila tracks its treatment actions on its own tracker: 14 of 22 are done with evidence, and eight are overdue with no new date. The tracker has never been reviewed.

Manila reports the Group's KPIs each quarter, with records, but has not set what else it monitors, by which methods, or who analyses and evaluates the results and when. The reports are filed; nobody reviews them or acts on them.
No internal audit of the Manila ISMS has been held and none is planned: there is no audit programme, no auditor named and no audit report.
No management review has covered the Manila ISMS, and none is scheduled. There are no minutes and no decisions on record.

Improvements are made one at a time, when a client asks or after an incident. Nothing records that the ISMS as a whole is being made more suitable, adequate or effective, and nobody is asked to look for improvements.
No nonconformity is identified or recorded at Manila: there is no log, no corrective-action procedure in use and nobody assigned to deal with nonconformities.

Manila keeps its own list of the policies in force there, a spreadsheet approved by the Org CISO in March 2026 with each policy's owner and last approval; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. Nothing records that the policies were communicated to the Manila workforce or acknowledged by it. Your POL-SET (T3.1) found two policies past their yearly review and no policy on endpoints.
A.5.2 Information security roles and responsibilities

The GRC Charter Section 16 sets the Group's GRC roles, with who is Responsible and Accountable for each core process, and SITL-POL-001 Section 5 gives each role its policy duties. At Manila, day-to-day ownership of the ISMS is not assigned to any role, and nothing at Manila records who holds which ISMS role. The Manila job descriptions say nothing about security responsibilities, and no record shows the ISMS roles were communicated to anyone.

No list of conflicting duties exists at Manila: nobody there has looked for them, and nothing says which duties must be kept apart. This sprint's walk-through in October 2026 found two, and its notes name who holds them: in the finance team of three, one person both creates suppliers in the supplier master and approves their payments, and nobody reviews changes to the supplier master; two network administrators approve their own firewall changes. Nothing is in place to separate these duties or to watch them.

Every Manila manager signs Manila's own manager security checklist when appointed and again each January: it lists the manager's security duties, and the Org CEO approved it in 2025. The 14 signed checklists are on file with Manila HR. Before a new agent is given system access, the team leader briefs them on their security role and both sign the briefing record; an access request without one is sent back. Managers require their staff to complete the induction security training, and attendance is recorded. No other office uses the checklist, and it has never been reviewed.

A.5.2 Information security roles and responsibilities
LI-RACI names 10 ISMS roles, one for each ISMS process. A holder is named at Manila for 7 of them, and 4 of those 7 have signed the role's responsibilities (Manila HR file).

The A.5.3 list holds 2 conflicting duties (CIT-S1). Since 12 October 2026 the procurement team creates suppliers, so the finance clerk only approves their payments. Since 2 November 2026 a second network administrator approves each firewall change.

A.5.22 Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services
