h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: A.5.9 Inventory of information and other associated assets

Manila's 81 assets are registered in the Group Information Asset Register, the inventory every office keeps under SITL-POL-003, the Group CIO's approved asset management policy; each has an owner role and a classification (the Manila extract is in Risk Register › Asset Register). Manila keeps its part up to date with the Group asset-change form of SITL-POL-003, the same in every office, and the Group CIO's office reviews the procedure each year. The Chief Information Officer reviewed Manila's part of the register in March 2026 and signed the review record. The half-yearly check of the register against what is really in use (SITL-ADD-16 Section 5) has never been run at Manila. This sprint's walk-through in October 2026 found two things in use that are not registered: a cloud CRM subscription the client relationship managers bought on a company card for their sales pipeline, and six loan laptops kept by the training team.
A.5.10 Acceptable use of information and other associated assets

SITL-POL-005, the Group's acceptable use policy, applies at Manila. New agents sign Manila's own acceptable-use form at induction, approved by the Org CISO in 2023; the signed forms are on file with Manila HR, one for each of the office's employees. The 38 contractors from two staffing agencies who work on the call floor sign nothing, and nobody has told them the rules. Agents handle client data as the Group handling matrix (SITL-STD-001 Section 6) sets, written into the call-floor procedures. No other office uses Manila's form, and it has never been reviewed.

Manila HR runs its own leaver checklist, approved by the HR & Workforce Management lead in 2025: each leaver hands back their headset, access card and, where issued, laptop, checked against the equipment issue log, and the team leader signs it on the last day. All 46 leavers since January 2026 have a signed checklist on file. The checklist asks team leaders and managers who leave for a handover note, and the notes are kept with it. No other office uses the checklist, and it has never been reviewed.

Manila classifies with SITL-STD-001, the Group's approved classification standard, as every office does: its label mapping turns the four tiers into GlobalConnect's labels (Public, Internal, Client-Confidential, Client-Restricted), and each registered asset has a label set by its owner. The owners review their classifications once a year, as Section 8 of the standard asks, and the Compliance Manager keeps the record: Manila's last review, in January 2026, is on file. No integrity or availability rating is recorded for any Manila asset. The healthcare-claims case files, taken on with the new healthcare clients in August 2026, were labelled Client-Confidential by their owner and have not been looked at since.

Manila's own labelling note, approved by the Org CISO in 2025, tells staff to type Client-Confidential in the footer of client documents. It covers documents only: e-mail, systems, paper and media are left out, and so is where a label may be left off. In the walk-through's sample of 20 documents and e-mails holding client data, 6 documents carried the label and no e-mail did; the e-mail system has no labels set up. Agents have never been trained to label. No other office uses the note, and it has never been reviewed.

Client files reach Manila through the production delivery platform's encrypted upload, as Manila's own secure file transfer guide says; the Head of Infrastructure approved the guide in 2024, no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. Each of the four external integrations of SITL-ADD-16 Section 9.1 is covered by a contract with a data protection agreement. One client still sends its weekly transaction file to a legacy FTP server at Manila, unencrypted. Calls and e-mails with clients follow the call-floor procedures.
The Group policies apply at Manila through SITL-ADD-16, and the Group requires every office to keep the policies in force approved, communicated and reviewed (SITL-POL-000 Section 7).
A.5.2 Information security roles and responsibilities
The Data Privacy Act 2012 requires Manila to appoint a Data Protection Officer (SITL-ADD-16 Section 2.1); the GRC Charter sets the Group's other ISMS roles.
The Manila risk register treats the risk of one person in the finance team of three creating a false supplier and paying it with this control.
The Group requires every manager to accept their security duties and to brief their people before access is given (SITL-POL-001 Section 5).
The Data Privacy Act 2012 requires serious personal data breaches to be notified to the National Privacy Commission within 72 hours (SITL-ADD-16 Section 2).
A.5.6 Contact with special interest groups
Manila needs early warning of threats aimed at the BPO sector, which the sector's information sharing and analysis centre (ISAC) gives its members.

Your risk treatment plan (LI-RTP, T5.1) treats risk R-16-HQ-16, the exploited flaw in the remote-access VPN, with this control: each new advisory on the VPN product, from the vendor and the sector ISAC, is taken into the risk assessment.
A.5.8 Information security in project management

Manila runs about six projects a year: client onboardings, customer-portal releases and infrastructure changes. NPC Advisory 2017-03 requires a Privacy Impact Assessment before each new BPO contract. Every project uses Manila's own project template, approved by the Org CISO in May 2025, and is logged in the project register with its stage-gate records; no other office uses the template, and it has never been reviewed. The template's security review is an optional box, ticked for 2 of the 6 projects of 2026, and only the SIEM's move to a hybrid set-up has a written security impact note. No project records security requirements for what it delivers, or who answers for security in it.
A.5.9 Inventory of information and other associated assets
The Group requires every office to keep its assets in the Group asset register, each with an owner, reviewed every year (SITL-ADD-16 Section 5, SITL-POL-003).
A.5.10 Acceptable use of information and other associated assets
Client data-protection agreements require agents to use client data, e-mail and the internet only for the client's service.
Agent turnover is high, and the Manila risk register treats the risk of leavers keeping laptops, headsets and building badges with this control.
Client data-protection agreements require client data to be handled by its classification; Manila labels it Client-Confidential or Client-Restricted (SITL-ADD-16 Section 7).
The Group requires every office to label information with its own label for each Group tier (SITL-ADD-16 Section 7).
Client contracts require end-customer data to pass to and from the client CRM tenants and payment gateways only over the agreed secure channels (SITL-ADD-16 Section 9.1).
The Manila risk register treats the risk of agents opening the accounts of clients they do not serve with this control.
Client data-protection agreements require every action on client data to be traced to one named agent, which the shared CRM log-ins on some accounts break (CTX-ISS-6).
The Manila risk register treats the risk of agents sharing passwords or writing them down at their workstations with this control.
PCI DSS, which the card-handling clients' contracts require, asks for access to card data to be granted by role and reviewed.
A.5.19 Information security in supplier relationships
Manila depends on suppliers for payroll, telecom, the CRM and identity checks; the Group requires every office to manage supplier risk from due diligence to exit (SITL-POL-013).
A.5.20 Addressing information security within supplier agreements
The Data Privacy Act 2012 requires a written agreement with every processor that handles personal data for Manila, the outside payroll provider among them.
A.5.21 Managing information security in the ICT supply chain
Manila buys its workstations, headsets and network equipment from IT vendors; the Manila risk register treats the risk of tampered or unsupported equipment with this control.
A.5.22 Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services
Nobody checks the payroll provider's work (GAP-25, 8.1); the Group requires critical suppliers to be reassessed every year (SITL-ADD-16 Section 5).
A.5.23 Information security for use of cloud services

Manila runs no cloud servers of its own, but its CRM, workforce management, VoIP and HR systems are cloud services (SaaS); client data-protection agreements require the security of these services to be assessed.
A.5.24 Information security incident management planning and preparation
The Data Privacy Act 2012 gives Manila 72 hours to notify the NPC and the people affected by a breach, which needs incident roles and steps prepared in advance.
A.5.25 Assessment and decision on information security events
The new financial-services client's security schedule requires any security incident affecting its data to be reported to it within 24 hours (Organization_Profiles Section 3).
A.5.26 Response to information security incidents
The Manila risk register treats the risk of a breach of client data spreading because the response is slow with this control.
A.5.27 Learning from information security incidents
The Group requires every office to review its incidents and feed the lessons back into its controls (SITL-POL-014).

The new financial-services client's security schedule requires a root-cause report within 5 working days of each incident affecting its data (Organization_Profiles Section 3), which rests on the evidence kept.
Client service-level schedules require operational uptime each month (SITL-ADD-16 Section 2.2), during an incident or an outage too.
A.5.30 ICT readiness for business continuity
The Manila risk register treats the risk of the data centre's core network failing during a typhoon with this control.
A.5.31 Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements
The Data Privacy Act 2012, the Cybercrime Prevention Act 2012 and the Labor Code of the Philippines all apply to the Manila office (SITL-ADD-16 Sections 2 and 4).
Manila sells no products of its own, but every workstation runs licensed software and the customer portal uses open-source components; the licence agreements set what may be installed and used.
The Data Privacy Act 2012 requires personal data to be kept no longer than its purpose needs; Manila keeps call recordings and client records.
A.5.34 Privacy and protection of personal identifiable information (PII)
The Data Privacy Act 2012 applies to the end-customer personal data Manila handles, and the National Privacy Commission is its lead regulator (SITL-ADD-16 Section 1).
A.5.35 Independent review of information security
Clients audit Manila's data-protection controls once a year under their data-protection agreements (CTX-ISS-6).
A.5.36 Compliance with policies, rules and standards for information security
The Group requires every office to measure compliance with its policies through KPIs, control testing and internal audit (SITL-POL-001 Section 8).
Manila's IT team runs the data centre, the backups and the call-recording servers; the Group requires operating procedures for them (SITL-POL-009).
Client contracts for the financial-services accounts require background checks on agents before they handle account data.
A.6.2 Terms and conditions of employment
The Group requires every employee's terms of employment to state their security responsibilities (SITL-POL-019).
A.6.3 Information security awareness, education and training
The Data Privacy Act 2012 requires annual privacy awareness training for all staff (SITL-ADD-16 Section 2.1); new agents are trained once, at induction (GAP-25, 7.3).
The Labor Code of the Philippines sets the due process Manila must follow before it disciplines an employee, a security breach included.
A.6.5 Responsibilities after termination or change of employment
Client data-protection agreements require agents' confidentiality duties to continue after they leave Manila.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: A.6.3 Information security awareness, education and training

Every new agent at Manila attends a one-hour security awareness session in their first week, from Manila's own slide deck, which the Org CISO approved in 2024; Manila HR keeps the signed attendance sheet of every session, for every agent who started in 2025 or 2026. There is no refresher: staff who joined before 2025 have had no awareness training since their own induction, and Manila has run no awareness campaign and no phishing simulation. Nothing checks what agents take away from the session: in the Org CISO's one-off spot check for the gap analysis, four of ten agents could not say where to report a suspicious call. No other office uses the deck, and it has never been reviewed.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: A.5.6 Contact with special interest groups

Manila keeps its own list of the special interest groups it belongs to, a spreadsheet approved by the Org CISO in May 2025: the BPO sector ISAC (information sharing and analysis centre), whose membership the Org CISO holds, and a national association of information security professionals, whose membership two GRC analysts hold. The Org CISO forwards each ISAC alert to the Head of Infrastructure or the team it concerns, and the forwarded alerts are kept with the action each team took. Manila's information-sharing note, approved with the list, says what may be shared with the ISAC (indicators of an attack, never client data), and the ISAC's duty contact is in the Manila incident contact list. No other office uses the list or the note, and neither has been reviewed.

The Group's Cyber Threat Intelligence Analyst collects threat information from the Group's vetted sources (its threat-intelligence platform and the BPO sector ISAC's feeds), analyses each item for each office's assets, and sends a threat-intelligence brief to every Org CISO each week, as the GRC Charter's reporting calendar (Section 15.1) sets; the Charter is reviewed each year. THR-5, of 26 October 2026, is the latest brief for Manila. At Manila the brief stops with the Org CISO: nobody passes its items on to the teams that run the affected systems or to the risk owners. Nothing at Manila takes the briefs into the risk assessment: no risk in the register cites a brief, and the register was last rated in March 2026. Nobody measures how the briefs are used.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: Manila's data-centre team works from 12 operating procedures, among them backup and restore, start-up and shutdown, patch deployment and log monitoring. They are pages on the Manila IT wiki, which the Chief Information Officer set up in 2024 as the place for the team's procedures, in a note he approved; every team member can open and edit them on shift, the wiki keeps each edit, and the team keeps them current and follows them. None is in the Group library: no page carries an ID, a version, an owner or an approval, a change goes live as soon as someone saves it, and nobody reviews the pages. No other office uses the wiki.

Screening at Manila follows the Group screening procedure of SITL-POL-019, which every Group organisation uses and the Group CHRO reviews each year. It sets the checks for each role band: identity, NBI clearance, education and previous employment for every role, and more for roles that handle client financial data. Manila HR has an outside screening provider run them before the start date, and the HR system keeps each report with its completion date: every new employee of 2026 was screened before starting. Agency contractors are screened by their agencies; the agency contracts do not require it, and Manila keeps no record of the results. In October an IT contractor joined the data-centre team eleven days before his agency's report arrived, with the team's full access, and nothing recorded it. Nobody measures how screening performs.
A.6.2 Terms and conditions of employment

Every Manila employee signs Manila's own employment contract before the start date; Manila HR drafted it with local counsel, and the Org CEO approved it in 2023. Its security clause sets the employee's duties (follow the Group's security policies, keep client information confidential, respect the Data Privacy Act of 2012) and GlobalConnect's (security training, and the equipment and access the work needs), and says that the confidentiality duty continues after employment ends. HR holds the signed contract of every employee, signed before their system access was granted. No other office uses this contract, and it has never been reviewed.

Manila HR's disciplinary procedure, approved by the HR & Workforce Management lead in 2025, covers any breach of a company policy, the information security policies included, with graduated penalties from a written warning to dismissal that weigh how serious the breach is and whether it is repeated; HR keeps a case file for each case. Staff are not told what happens if they breach an information security policy: nothing communicates that such breaches fall under the procedure. In 2026 team leaders gave verbal warnings to agents found sharing their CRM log-ins outside the procedure, each in their own way, with no check that a breach had happened and no case recorded. No other office uses the procedure, and it has never been reviewed.
A.6.5 Responsibilities after termination or change of employment

At the exit interview Manila HR gives each leaver a letter restating the duties that continue after they leave: client and company information stays confidential, work products remain GlobalConnect's, and the confidentiality clause of their contract still binds them. The leaver signs a copy, kept with the leaver checklist: 46 signed copies since January 2026. When someone changes role, the mover form ends the old role's duties, sets the new ones, restates the same continuing duties and goes to both team leaders; the mover signs it. Manila HR wrote both, and the HR & Workforce Management lead approved them in 2025. No other office uses them, and they have never been reviewed.

Employees' confidentiality is in their contracts. Manila's confidentiality agreement template, written by its legal counsel and approved by the Org CEO in 2024, covers client and company information during the work and for five years after, and sets the remedies for a breach. Every supplier that receives client data signs it before access, and the signed agreements are on file. Manila's counsel reviews the template each year, and the 2026 review is on file. The agency contractors sign no confidentiality agreement, and the agency contracts hold none. No other office uses the template.

About 40 night-shift supervisors and IT on-call staff work from home on some shifts. They use company laptops with encrypted disks and reach the Manila network only through the remote-access VPN, with multi-factor authentication; the IT team's monthly device and VPN reports list both for each of them. Remote working is set by the Group remote-working rules, approved by the Group GRC Steering Committee, the same in every office and reviewed each year by the Group CISO's office: they say who may work from home and on which equipment, but not from where or how client information is to be protected there. Team leaders hand them over when someone starts working from home, and nothing records that these remote workers read or accepted them. Nothing is measured against a target. The VPN gateway itself carries risk R-16-HQ-16, which your risk treatment plan (T5.1) treats.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: A.5.19 Information security in supplier relationships

Manila tiers and assesses its suppliers by the Group supplier procedure of SITL-POL-013, which the Group GRC Steering Committee approved and every GlobalConnect office uses; the Group reviews it each year. The vendor register records each supplier's business owner, tier, last assessment date and contract dates, and each supplier's tiering and assessment records are dated before its contract, Deskline Cloud's of 2025 among them. When a supplier leaves, it is closed by the offboarding procedure: in 2026 two suppliers left, each with its access removed on the end date and a deletion certificate on file.
A.5.20 Addressing information security within supplier agreements

Since SITL-POL-013 took effect, Procurement / Legal draft every new contract from the Group clause checklist for the supplier's tier (Section 6.1, step 4), which the Group GRC Steering Committee approved and every office uses; the Group reviews the checklist each year. VeriPass's draft is the first read against it at Manila, in your VEN-CL. The contracts signed before it, Deskline Cloud's in 2025 and PayWise's in 2023, were signed on the supplier's terms and have not been brought up to the checklist, and nothing records a decision on their gaps.
A.5.21 Managing information security in the ICT supply chain

The Group supplier questionnaire (rule R27), which the Group GRC Steering Committee approved and every office sends, asks each High and Critical supplier to list the sub-processors that can access its data, and the answers are kept with its assessment; the Group reviews the questionnaire each year. Deskline Cloud listed its sub-processors at its 2025 assessment; the support-chat provider it added in October 2026 is not on Manila's record. No agreement requires a supplier to pass Manila's security requirements on to the suppliers it uses, and the questionnaire does not ask how the software and updates a supplier delivers are checked.
A.5.22 Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services

Nothing at Manila sets when a supplier is reviewed or reassessed: the Vendor / Third-Party Risk Analyst reassesses suppliers as they come to mind, from the last assessment date in the vendor register, and no supplier service reviews are held. Of the reassessments that fell due in the last 12 months, four were done by their due date; the payroll provider's and a telecom carrier's are overdue. Supplier incident reports and change notices, such as Deskline Cloud's notice of a new sub-processor in September 2026, are filed without being assessed.
A.5.23 Information security for use of cloud services

Cloud services at Manila are approved with Manila IT's own cloud checklist, written by the Chief Information Officer in 2024; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. The Group approval procedure of SITL-POL-021 Section 6.1 and its cloud service register, which the Group GRC Steering Committee approved for every office, have not been brought in at Manila yet. Deskline Cloud, the SaaS ticketing tool of the service desk, was bought by Service Delivery in 2025, before that policy took effect, and has been through neither: no architecture review, no shared-responsibility matrix and no entry in the cloud service register. Manila IT connected it to Manila's single sign-on and sends its audit log to the SIEM each week. There is no exit plan for it: its terms let Manila export its data as CSV files for 30 days after the contract ends.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: The office's perimeter is set by the Group facilities security procedures under SITL-POL-008, the same in every GlobalConnect office, and the Group Head of Facilities reviews how each office applies them every year (Manila: June 2026). The walls run from the floor to the concrete slab with no gap above the ceiling, and the main doors and the goods entrance are kept shut and open only by badge. On the walkthrough the fire exit to the stairwell was wedged open, and its door alarm was isolated at the panel. Nothing is measured against a target.

Entry is set by Manila's own entry and visitor procedure, written by the facilities team and approved by the Org CISO in 2024; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. The main doors, the goods entrance and each secure area open only by badge, and the badge system logs every entry; the list of badges issued and a six-month extract of the entry log were exported for this sprint. Deliveries are left in a caged room by the service lift and do not reach the office. Visitors sign the visitor book and wear a visitor badge, but escorts are not enforced: the walkthrough saw two visitors alone on the agent floor, as the September spot check had. SITL-ADD-16 Section 5 asks for a secure-area access review every six months; none has been held at Manila. Nothing is measured against a target.
A.7.3 Securing offices, rooms and facilities

The server room, the records room and the IT store are inside the perimeter, away from the reception and the lift lobby, and each is locked: by badge (server room, IT store) or keypad (records room). Their doors carry room numbers only, with nothing to say what is inside, and the building directory lists GlobalConnect by floor alone. Manila facilities keeps the list of these rooms, with each one's lock and who holds a badge or the code. This is how the Group facilities security procedures under SITL-POL-008 set it, the same in every office and reviewed every year by the Group Head of Facilities; nothing is measured against a target.

Manila has its own CCTV procedure, approved by the Manila facilities manager in 2024: 24 cameras, recordings kept for 30 days on a recorder that only the facilities manager and the Org CISO can view, and an intruder alarm on the floor outside office hours, monitored by the building's security desk. The camera layout lists each camera and what it covers: the main doors, the goods entrance, the fire exit and the server room door are covered; the IT store door is not. The alarm is tested each quarter, with records. No other office uses the procedure, and it has never been reviewed.
A.7.5 Protecting against physical and environmental threats

The site threat assessment of June 2026 covers fire, typhoon, street flooding, earthquake and power loss, by the Group facilities security procedures under SITL-POL-008, the same in every office and reviewed every year by the Group Head of Facilities. The server room has smoke detection and a gas fire-suppression system, inspected in May 2026. The room sits directly below the floor 13 staff kitchen, which the assessment does not mention, and it has no water detection; there is a water stain on a ceiling tile above rack 3. Nothing is measured against a target.

The Group facilities security procedures under SITL-POL-008, the same in every office and reviewed every year by the Group Head of Facilities, set the rules for the secure areas, posted on each door: no photography or recording without IT approval. Contractors and visitors sign the secure-area sheet and are escorted by IT throughout, with the escort's name recorded, and the facilities team checks every evening that the secure areas are locked, on a signed check sheet. Nothing is measured against a target.
A.7.7 Clear desk and clear screen

Manila works to its own clear desk and clear screen rule, written by the facilities team and approved by the Org CISO in 2025; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. Screens lock after 5 minutes idle, set centrally on every workstation, and the setting was exported for this sprint; printing is released only by the badge reader on the printer; team leaders check the desks each evening against a checklist, with signed records. The checklist does not cover the meeting rooms: the walkthrough found a whiteboard listing a client's customer names and account numbers, left from the day before. Nothing is measured against a target.

Equipment is sited by the Group IT security procedures, the same in every office and reviewed every year by the Group CIO's office. The server racks are locked, in the server room, where no food or drink is allowed. The agent floor's screens face away from the windows and the corridor, but three workstations beside the reception glass face the visitor seats, and their screens show customer records. No list records where the equipment that handles client data is sited. Nothing is measured against a target.

Laptops taken home by team leaders and managers are issued by the Group IT security procedures, the same in every office and reviewed every year by the Group CIO's office. The IT desk keeps the off-site device register: each laptop with its asset tag, holder, the manager's approval and its encryption status; all 46 are encrypted. Each holder signs the Group remote-working rules, which forbid leaving a laptop unattended in a car or a public place. Nothing is measured against a target.

Removable media follow the Group IT security procedures and the handling matrix of SITL-STD-001 Section 6, the same in every office and reviewed every year by the Group CIO's office. USB storage is blocked on the agent workstations; the IT desk issues Group encrypted drives, keeps a register of the 12 issued, and stores them in a locked drawer when not in use. The meeting-room PCs are not blocked: the walkthrough found an unlabelled USB stick left in one, not encrypted and not in the register. Nothing is measured against a target.

The server room runs on a UPS with about 30 minutes of battery, backed by the building's generator, and its cooling is monitored and alarms to the IT on-call. By the Group IT security procedures, the same in every office and reviewed every year by the Group CIO's office, the UPS is serviced every six months (last in August 2026) and the building management tests the generator each month, with the test sheets kept by IT. IT keeps the list of the utilities the office depends on and the backup for each. Nothing is measured against a target.

Cabling follows the IT team's own cabling standard, approved by the Chief Information Officer in 2024; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. In the server room, power and network cables run in separate labelled trays under the raised floor. The agent floor's patch panel sits in an open rack in the corridor by the meeting rooms, with no door and with unlabelled cables, and no drawing of the cable routes exists for the floor. Nothing is measured against a target.

The UPS, the cooling units and the PBX are maintained under supplier contracts at the intervals the suppliers set, by the Group IT security procedures, the same in every office and reviewed every year by the Group CIO's office. IT keeps the maintenance schedule with each item's last service, and the suppliers' signed service reports; equipment sent away for repair has its disks removed first, recorded on the dispatch sheet. Nothing is measured against a target.
A.7.14 Secure disposal or re-use of equipment

Disposal follows the IT team's own disposal procedure, approved by the Chief Information Officer in 2024; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. Under it, storage is cleared as the handling matrix of SITL-STD-001 Section 6 sets for its tier, by a certified destruction supplier, with a certificate. IT's disposal log lists every device disposed of or re-used in the last 12 months, and the supplier's certificates for the two server batches of 2025 are on file. In March 2026, 12 old team-leader laptops that had held client data were given to staff to keep after a quick format, with no wipe record. In the IT store a locked cage holds returned laptops and loose disks awaiting disposal, unlabelled and with no list of what is in it. Nothing is measured against a target.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: Manila's business continuity plan, its own document approved by the Org CEO in 2025, moves agents to the second Manila site or to work from home when a centre is lost. For information security during a disruption it sets two rules: at the recovery site agents sign in to the CRM only through the IAM, and at home they use company laptops over the VPN. The full DR failover test of 13 June 2026 logged that the SIEM collected no logs from the recovery site for its first six hours; nobody followed it up, and the plan was not changed. No other office uses the plan, and it has never been reviewed.
A.5.30 ICT readiness for business continuity

Manila's business impact analysis follows the Group procedure of SITL-POL-015 Section 6.1, as every office's does: refreshed in March 2026 and approved by the Org CEO, it sets an RTO and an RPO for each of five services (dataset BIA-5). Corporate IT keeps a disaster recovery runbook for each service on the Group template, with its recovery steps and who carries them out; the Group reviews the procedure and the template each year. The full DR failover test of 13 June 2026 ran on the Group test procedure, and your BIA-RTO (step 1) holds its results against the objectives. For the objectives it missed, no remediation is planned and no retest is booked. Nothing is measured against a target.
A.5.31 Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements

Manila's obligations are kept on the Group's obligations register template, T-OBL, in the Group GRC tool, as every office's are, and the Group Compliance Manager reviews each office's register every year; the review of Manila's in October 2026 is on record. Your OBL-REG (step 3) is its extract for the obligations SITL-ADD-16 sets, each with its type and owner; SITL-ADD-16 Section 2.2 gives each one's article, deadline, process and evidence of compliance. The register holds none of the client contracts' requirements. The Group logs regulatory changes each month under SITL-POL-016 Section 6.1, but nothing at Manila records that any change was assessed for the office. Client data leaves the Philippines only under the accountability principle the addendum names, and agents use only the encryption IT provides: both rules are followed. Nothing is measured against a target.

Manila's IT team keeps its own software licence register for the call-centre workstations, a spreadsheet approved by the Head of Infrastructure and updated at every purchase; software is bought only through the Group's approved resellers. Agents have no administrator rights, so only IT installs software. The January 2026 licence count found 1,240 workstation licences for 1,180 installations. The induction security training covers SITL-POL-005's rule not to copy or use software or material without a licence, with attendance recorded. No other office uses the register, and it has never been reviewed.

The retention schedule of SITL-POL-018, the Group's records policy, applies at Manila as in every office: each type of record with its retention period, and the Group reviews it each year. Paper records are shredded by a contractor, and its certificate of destruction is kept for each collection. Call recordings, though, stay on the call recording servers for as long as disk space allows, about 14 months, whatever the schedule and each client's data-protection agreement say. Any QA supervisor can delete a recording, and deletions are not logged. Nothing is measured against a target.
A.5.34 Privacy and protection of personal identifiable information (PII)

SITL-POL-017 applies at Manila through SITL-ADD-16. The privacy rules are taught once, in the induction security training; there is no yearly privacy awareness training, which SITL-ADD-16 Section 2.1 requires. Manila's DPO is appointed and registered with the NPC, and its data processing systems are registered, renewed in March 2026. Manila keeps its record of processing activities in its own spreadsheet, one entry per activity with its lawful basis, approved by the DPO; no other office uses its layout, and it has never been reviewed. Your ROPA (step 3) is the customer-support activity's entry, on the Group template T-ROPA, with its DPIA screening. The healthcare-claims work that began in August 2026 was not screened for a DPIA before it started.
A.5.35 Independent review of information security

No internal audit has covered the Manila ISMS (your LI-GAP, Clause 9.2). Since 2025 Manila has had an external security firm review its client-data controls once a year, an arrangement of its own approved by the Org CEO; the 2025 and 2026 reports went to the Org CEO and are on file. The firm reviews only the client-data controls: no plan says which other areas of the office's information security are reviewed, or when, and nobody tracks what the reports recommend. The Manila IT manager also runs a quarterly self-check of the IT controls he operates. No other office has such an arrangement, and it has never been reviewed.
A.5.36 Compliance with policies, rules and standards for information security

Each quarter, Manila team leaders run the Group compliance checklist on their floor (clean desk, screen lock, the call-recording rules), as team leaders do in every office, and the Group reviews the checklist each year. The results go into the Group GRC tool and to the Org CISO. Each failure gets a cause and a corrective action with an owner, and the Org CISO checks it at the next round: floor 3 failed the clean-desk check in the second quarter for want of lockable drawers, which were fitted, and passed in the third. Nothing is measured against a target.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: Manila keeps its own hardening checklist for each of its systems, approved by the Head of Infrastructure in 2025, giving each setting's baseline and the SITL rule it carries out; no other office uses the checklists, and they have never been reviewed. Each system was built to its checklist, and the build records are kept. Nothing checks the configurations after a build: there is no drift monitoring, and firewall rules are changed without a change ticket (dataset NET, rule R-04). Your CFG-BASE (step 1) checked 12 settings of six systems against their checklists.

Information is deleted under the Group's records retention and disposal policy SITL-POL-018, the way every office does it, and the Group reviews the procedure each year. Disks and devices leaving Manila are crypto-erased or shredded by a certified contractor, by the method SITL-STD-001 Section 6 sets for their tier, and every disposal in 2026 has its certificate on file. Client data is deleted at the end of each contract, with a signed deletion record. Nothing is measured.

The Group data-masking procedure, issued under SITL-POL-017, is used in every office and reviewed each year: it says which fields are masked and how. The CRM test tenant is refreshed each quarter with masked copies, and every masking run is logged. In September 2026 the delivery team copied a production extract of client transaction data, with end-customers' names and account numbers, to the test system without masking it; nothing stopped the copy, and nobody checks copies before they are used. Copies are requested by e-mail, and no register lists the copies made out of production. Nothing is measured.

Manila runs its own data-leakage rules on the e-mail gateway, approved by the Org CISO in 2025: e-mails carrying a Client-Restricted label or a card number to an outside address are blocked, and every block is logged. USB storage is blocked on every workstation. No other office uses these rules, and they have never been reviewed. Uploads to websites and exports from the CRM are not monitored. Nobody looks at the logged blocks or acts on them.
A.8.18 Use of privileged utility programs

Privileged utilities (registry and disk editors, packet capture, database consoles) run only through the Group PAM, from the Group's list of approved utilities, which every office uses. Each run needs a ticket approved by the system's owner, and every session is recorded. Utilities not on the list are removed from server builds. The quarterly privileged access review checks the list, and the Group reviews the procedure each year. Nothing is measured.
A.8.19 Installation of software on operational systems

Only Manila's server administrators install software on servers, each time through a change ticket approved by the Head of Infrastructure, and only software on Manila's own approved software list, approved in 2025. Agents and team leaders have no administrator rights, so they cannot install software on their workstations. Every installation is recorded in the change log. No other office uses the list, and it has never been reviewed.

The Group network security policy SITL-POL-011 applies in every office; it was last approved on 29 September 2025, and its yearly review has not been held. At Manila the network devices are managed only from the management zone, and the firewall and switch logs go to the SIEM, where alerts are watched in business hours with on-call alerting. Traffic to Warsaw runs over an encrypted site-to-site VPN. Inside the office, the agent floor reaches the file shares on FS-MNL-01 without encryption, though the files are Client-Confidential.

Manila's network services come from two telecom carriers. Their contracts, on the Group template under SITL-POL-011, set each service's security features (encrypted links, protection against denial-of-service attacks) and its service levels. SITL-POL-011's yearly review has not been held since its approval on 29 September 2025. The carriers send monthly service reports, but nobody at Manila reads them, and one carrier's reassessment is overdue.

The Manila network is divided into six zones under the Group network security policy SITL-POL-011, as in every office: guest Wi-Fi, agent floor, server zone, security zone, card-data zone and management (dataset NET). The firewall's rule base records what may pass between them. SITL-POL-011's yearly review has not been held since its approval on 29 September 2025. All traffic between zones passes the core firewall FW-MNL-01. Its rule R-04, added in November 2025 for a client demonstration with no change ticket and no end date, allows any traffic from the guest Wi-Fi to the server zone.

All web traffic from the office, guest Wi-Fi included, goes through the Group web proxy, which every office uses. It blocks the malware, phishing and gambling categories, the provider updates its category list daily, and every block is logged. The Group reviews the filtering rules each year, with SITL-POL-005. Nothing is measured.

The Group cryptography policy SITL-POL-007 applies in every office; the Group reviewed it and approved version 1.3 on 4 November 2026, and SITL-STD-001 Section 6 sets what each tier needs. At Manila the CA keys are in the HSM and the client transaction data key is in the cloud KMS, each with its rotation recorded. The call recording archive database key is kept in a plain-text file on the same server as the database and has never been rotated. Nothing records that retired keys were destroyed, and nothing is measured.

THR-5.note: Threat-intelligence brief for GlobalConnect Customer Solutions, Manila, 26 October 2026, from the Group's Cyber Threat Intelligence Analyst to the Org CISO (the weekly brief of the GRC Charter Section 15.1). Five items, each with its source and what it means for the office.
h: What it means for the Manila office
r: Pretext calls to call-centre agents: callers pose as a client's customer or as IT support to have account details changed or a password reset. Rising across the BPO sector since July 2026.
Manila's agents take customer calls on the CRM platforms. Already on the register: R-16-HQ-02, phishing and business-email compromise.

Active exploitation of a flaw in the remote-access VPN product the Manila office runs: attackers get into the network through unpatched gateways without valid credentials. Attacks on unpatched gateways of this product are reported several times a year across the sector, more often since the advisory. The vendor issued a fix on 14 October 2026.
The VPN vendor's security advisory, 14 October 2026; BPO sector ISAC bulletin, October 2026
Manila's remote-access VPN gateway runs the affected version. Night-shift supervisors and IT on-call staff reach the network only through it.
A ransomware group targeting BPO providers through their remote-support tools, then moving into their clients' environments.
Manila supports its clients' delivery platforms. Already on the register: R-16-HQ-01, ransomware disrupting Mission Critical services.
Interception of files sent to BPO providers over plain FTP: attackers on the network path read the files and the passwords sent with them. Reported at BPO providers in the region about once a year.
One client still sends its weekly transaction file to Manila's legacy FTP server without encryption.
Hacktivist DDoS campaigns against the public-facing services of companies in the Philippines, timed with regional tensions.
Manila's public-facing services are in reach. Already on the register: R-16-HQ-08, DDoS and hacktivist campaigns.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: SITL-POL-006, the Group's access control policy, applies at Manila through SITL-ADD-16: access is given on least privilege and need-to-know, with the asset owner's approval. It is approved by the Group GRC Steering Committee, the same in every office, and reviewed every year; nothing is measured at Manila. Manila has written no access rules for its systems: nobody has set which role gets which access on the CRM, the WFM or the call-recording and QA platform, or who approves it. A new starter is given the access of a colleague in the same team, and nobody has compared what each role holds with what its work needs.

Identities at Manila are created by the Group IAM from the HR joiner record, one per person, and disabled from the HR leaver record; the CRM and the call-recording and QA platform take their accounts from it, through single sign-on. The steps around the IAM are Manila's own: the Manila identity runbook, approved by the Org CISO in 2024, says who raises the joiner record, how an account name is formed and who checks a leaver's accounts; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. Nothing is measured. Two things sit outside it. The WFM's accounts are created and removed by hand by the WFM administrator, when a team leader e-mails. And on one client's account, five after-hours agents sign in to one CRM account named "support", created by the CRM administrator in 2025 so that the night shift could pick up the queue without signing in and out at handovers: its password is shared and its second factor is on the night team's shared phone. Nobody approved it, it is in no register, and nothing records which agent did what under it. The client complained about shared log-ins on 4 November 2026.

The CRM and the call-recording and QA platform sign in through the Group's single sign-on, with multi-factor authentication. The WFM, the Group's tenant set up the same for every office, has its own sign-in: each account gets a one-time enrolment link, must set a new password at first sign-in under the Group password rules (12 characters or more), and uses an authenticator app as its second factor. First passwords for directory accounts are issued through the Group IAM's self-service enrolment and must be changed at first sign-in. At enrolment the Group IAM shows every user, employees and agency contractors alike, the Group's rules for their password and second factor (keep them secret, never share them, report one that is disclosed), and the account opens only once the user accepts them; the IAM keeps each acceptance. This is the Group's way, the same in every office, and SITL-POL-006 is reviewed every year; nothing is measured at Manila.

Manila has no written way of its own for granting or reviewing access, and does not yet work to SITL-POL-006 Section 6, in force since 1 October 2026. A team leader asks the system's administrator by e-mail or chat, and the administrator grants what is asked; no approval by the asset owner is kept. The CRM was last reviewed in March 2025, by the CRM administrator, who holds an account on it, and the review was not signed; the WFM and the call-recording and QA platform have never been reviewed. When someone leaves, the HR leaver record disables the directory account through the Group IAM, with the time logged (the IAM disable log): from 1 September to 13 November 2026, 14 of 15 leavers were disabled within the SLA, the fifteenth, an involuntary leaver, after 3 hours. The WFM's accounts are outside the IAM, and are removed only when a team leader asks: the agent who left on 13 November still has one.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: The authority for Manila is the National Privacy Commission (NPC): your interested parties (CTX-IP, F1.3) list it among the regulators, with their requirements, and SITL-POL-014 Section 6.2 and the addendum's Section 2 say who notifies it and when. The Group DPO network keeps the authority contact list for every office, with the named contacts at the NPC and at the national cybercrime centre, and checks it each quarter; the September 2026 check is recorded. Manila's one notifiable breach of 2025 was notified to the NPC 51 hours after discovery, and the submission receipt is on file. The list and the procedure are the Group's, approved with SITL-POL-014 by the Group GRC Steering Committee, used in every office and reviewed yearly. Nobody counts the notifications made on time.
A.5.24 Information security incident management planning and preparation

Manila's incident response plan follows the Group template of SITL-POL-014: it names the incident team, each member's role and the call tree, and sets out the Group's procedures from reporting to post-incident review (Sections 6.1 to 6.3). The Org CISO approved it in October 2026, as every office approves its plan each year. The call tree was replaced in July 2026, yet at the tabletop of 24 November 2026 (dataset TTX) it still listed a team leader who left in August. That tabletop was the first held at Manila, and no member of the incident team has a training record for the plan. Nobody measures how ready the team is.
A.5.25 Assessment and decision on information security events

Every event reported to the service desk or the SOC is logged in the Group incident tool and assessed by the SOC analyst on duty, named on the SOC rota, against the severity scale of SITL-POL-014 Section 3.1 (SEV1 Critical to SEV4 Low, by the impact on safety, service, data, finance and reputation), within the hour Section 6.1 sets. The tool records each decision, incident or not, with its reason: 312 events were assessed at Manila from January to October 2026, and 5 of them were confirmed as incidents. The scale and the triage procedure are the Group's, approved with SITL-POL-014 by the Group GRC Steering Committee, used in every office and reviewed yearly. Nobody measures how long assessments take.
A.5.26 Response to information security incidents

Manila responds to incidents with its own runbook, written by the Manila IT manager in 2024 and approved by the Org CISO; the response team follows it. No other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. The incident tool shows each of the 5 incidents of 2026 contained, with every action logged. The 2 SEV2 incidents were not escalated to the Crisis Management Team or the Group CISO within the hour SITL-POL-014 Section 3.1 sets, and the runbook names nobody to tell clients or the authorities. The IT manager closes each incident in the tool, with no sign-off.
A.5.27 Learning from information security incidents

Post-incident reviews at Manila use the IT manager's own review template, approved by the Org CISO in 2024; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. The Group's template and procedure (SITL-POL-014 Section 6.1, step 6) have not been brought in. Manila held one for each of its 2 SEV2 incidents of 2026, within 10 working days, and both reports record the root cause and the lessons. The actions the reports propose have no owner or date, and nothing tracks them: the 2025 phishing incident's lesson was proposed again in 2026. Nobody at Manila counts incidents by type, volume or cost, or looks for those that recur.

Manila IT collects evidence by its own evidence-handling checklist, which the IT manager wrote in 2025 from SITL-POL-014 Sections 3.1 and 7.1 (preserve before changing anything, and keep the chain of custody) and the Org CISO approved; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed. Manila IT filled in a chain-of-custody form for each of the 2 SEV2 incidents of 2026: who took the disk image and the logs, when, and where they are kept. No hash was taken of any image or log when it was collected, so nothing shows they are unchanged, and nobody at Manila who collects evidence has been trained to do it. Nothing is measured.

Staff report suspected events to the service desk or the security hotline, as SITL-POL-014 Section 3.1 requires: the route, approved with the policy by the Group GRC Steering Committee, is on the Group intranet page that every office uses, reviewed yearly, and the service desk logs each report in the incident tool and passes it to the SOC. Manila's induction session does not say how to report an event, and there is no refresher (A.6.3, T6.1): in the Org CISO's spot check, four of ten agents could not say where to report a suspicious call. Nobody measures how quickly events are reported.

h: What was observed at the Manila office
r: No Group policy covers user endpoint devices: your POL-SET (T3.1) found it Missing. Manila IT keeps its own workstation and laptop build standard, approved by the Manila IT manager in 2024: disk encryption, screen lock after 5 minutes idle, no local administrator rights for users. The device management console reports 612 of Manila's 640 devices on the current build; the other 28 are call-floor workstations waiting for a rebuild. The laptops can be wiped remotely. Users sign nothing about their devices, and nothing says what to do when a laptop is lost. No other office uses the build standard, and it has never been reviewed.

Manila's 23 administrator accounts are held in the Group privileged access management (PAM) system, the way every office holds them under SITL-POL-006. Each is a separate administrator account, approved by the system owner and the Org CISO, checked out for one session at a time with multi-factor authentication, and the PAM system records the sessions on the 10 Mission Critical systems. The Org CISO's quarterly reviews of the accounts for Q1 to Q3 2026 are signed and on file. The Group reviews the PAM process every year, last in June 2026. Nothing is measured against a target.

Agents reach client records through the CRM platforms (Salesforce, HelpLoop). There Manila's own role matrix, approved by the Head of Security & Privacy in 2025, limits each team to its own clients' accounts, and the CRM settings match it. On the Manila file server, the folder of client KYC scans opens to every Manila user: the walk-through's permission report of October 2026 found it shared with the group All staff. No other office uses the role matrix, and it has never been reviewed.

The code of the in-house customer portal is kept in a Git repository. Manila's own access list for it, approved by the Manila development lead in 2025, gives write access to the portal's developers and read access to its two testers; write access is given only on the lead's approval, and the repository's settings match the list. Every change goes through the repository with its author recorded, and the repository logs every access. No other office uses the access list, and it has never been reviewed.

Every Manila user signs in through the Group identity provider (Identity & access management, a Mission Critical asset at Manila), which applies the Group's authentication standard under SITL-POL-006 the same way in every office: multi-factor authentication for every user, for remote access and for administrators, accounts locked after five failed attempts, sessions closed after 15 minutes idle, and every log-on recorded. The enrolment report shows every Manila user enrolled. The Group reviewed the standard in May 2026. Nothing is measured against a target.

Manila IT records the disk, memory and network use of its on-premises servers and the telephony lines each month, in a spreadsheet that the Head of Infrastructure approved as Manila's capacity procedure in 2025. Nothing projects future needs: no plan exists for the call volumes in the clients' service-level schedules for 2027, and the call recording servers reached 94% of their storage in October 2026 before more was added. No other office uses the procedure, and it has never been reviewed.

Every Manila server and workstation runs the Group's endpoint detection and response (EDR) service, run by Group security operations the same way in every office under SITL-POL-009 Section 3.2: signatures update by themselves, users cannot switch it off, and each detection is sent to the SIEM and handled by Group security operations. The EDR console shows 638 of Manila's 640 devices reporting in the last 7 days; the other two are away for repair. Mail and web traffic is scanned at the Group gateways, and staff learn about malware in the yearly awareness course. The Group reviewed the service in April 2026. Nothing is measured against a target.

The Group vulnerability team scans Manila's assets, authenticated: internet-facing ones every week and the rest every month, as SITL-POL-010 Section 3.1 sets. Its coverage report for October 2026 lists every registered Manila asset as scanned, with the date of each scan. The findings stay in the scanner, and Manila IT patches what it is e-mailed about, following the patch deployment page of its IT wiki. Nobody at Manila classifies the findings, sets their due dates or checks that a later scan confirms a fix, nothing records it, and no monthly SLA report has ever been made. Your VUL-TEST (step 1) is the first test of remediation against the timescales.

Manila's data-centre team backs up the on-premises servers every night to the backup server, and every week to the Group's cloud backup vault, kept apart from the office network. The schedule for each server is set in Manila's own backup standard, approved by the Head of Infrastructure in 2024; how to run the jobs and the restore test is the data-centre backup and restore page of the Manila IT wiki, which the Group CIO approved on 10 November 2026 as Manila's procedure for SITL-POL-009 Section 6.2. The job logs for August to October 2026 show every job completed. The DR test of 13 June 2026 failed over to replicas at the Group recovery site and restored no backup: no backup copy has been restored in a test in the last 12 months, though SITL-ADD-16 Section 5 sets a semi-annual restore test for Manila under SITL-POL-009. No other office uses the backup standard, and it has never been reviewed.
A.8.14 Redundancy of information processing facilities

Your BIA-RTO (T8.2) gives each Manila service the time within which it must be back. The DR test of 13 June 2026 moved the services to the Group recovery site. Inside the Manila data centre, Manila's own network design, approved by the Head of Infrastructure in 2025, pairs the two firewalls, and their failover was tested the same day. The core switch, the PBX and the call recording servers are single units: the core network and the telephony at the Manila data centre have no second path, so the failure of one of them means moving to the recovery site. No other office uses the design, and it has never been reviewed.

Manila's servers and network devices log log-ons, administrator actions, failures and security events, as Manila IT's own logging checklist sets; the Manila IT manager approved it in 2025. The logs stay on each device for 7 days and are then overwritten. Only the 10 Mission Critical systems also send theirs to the SIEM, which keeps them for 90 days. A server's administrators can delete its logs. No other office uses the checklist, and it has never been reviewed.

The SIEM at Manila (a Mission Critical asset) watches the 10 Mission Critical systems with alert rules written by Manila's security analysts, approved by the Head of Security & Privacy in 2025. Since November 2026 the remote-access VPN gateway also sends its logs, under your risk treatment plan (T5.1); the customer portal and the e-mail gateway, both internet-facing, send none. Two analysts review alerts from 08:00 to 17:00 on weekdays, and their review sheets are kept; nobody is alerted outside those hours. No other office uses the alert rules, and they have never been reviewed.

Every Manila server, network device and the SIEM take their time from the Group's two reference time servers, set the same way in every office under SITL-POL-009 Section 3.4 and the Group's time-source standard. The SIEM's time-offset report for November 2026 shows no system more than one second out, and it alerts on drift. The Group reviewed the setting in March 2026. Nothing is measured against a target.

What was observed at the Manila office
r: The portal team develops to SITL-POL-012, the Group Secure Development Lifecycle Policy (last approved June 2026), the life cycle of every Group organisation that builds software, reviewed each year by the Security Architecture & Standards Manager. Its security gates are set for each release in the pipeline that dataset SDLC describes, and the release records of 2026 show each of the 14 releases passing them. The repositories and the pipeline are open to the portal team alone, with sign-in through the Group's identity platform. Nothing is measured.

For each portal feature the product owner adds security acceptance criteria to the user story from the Group's application security checklist (SITL-POL-012), used by every Group organisation that builds software and reviewed each year, and the Security Architecture & Standards Manager approves them at sprint planning. The criteria are tested in QA before each release. The checklist has no items for card payments: the requirements for the payment page that PCI DSS sets, and that the card-handling clients' contracts require, have never been written down for it. Nothing is measured.
A.8.27 Secure system architecture and engineering principles

The engineering principles are the portal team's own: a one-page set the Manila architect wrote in 2024, approved by the Org CISO and reviewed each year at the team's yearly retrospective. No other office uses them, and they have never been compared with the Group reference architecture (SITL-TECH-000 Section 2). Every portal design change that alters a data flow or an integration is reviewed against them by the Manila architect before it is built: the 5 design reviews of 2026 are on file, each signed, with the principles checked. Nothing is measured.

The portal team codes to the Group's secure coding essentials (SITL-POL-012 Section 7.1), the standard of every Group organisation that writes software, reviewed each year. Every merge request needs a second developer's review, and the build runs a static code scan and a check of the open-source libraries; a High finding stops the build. In 2026 the Manila development lead waived 3 High findings to meet release dates, and no reason or approval is recorded for any of them. Five of the nine developers had secure coding training in the 2025 round; the four who joined in 2026 have had none. Nothing is measured.
A.8.29 Security testing in development and acceptance

The portal team tests each release at the Group's security test gate (SITL-POL-012 Section 6.1), used by every Group organisation that builds software and reviewed each year: a dynamic scan of the QA environment and tests of sign-in and session handling, with the results attached to the release ticket. The product owner signs off each release against its acceptance criteria. The portal's last penetration test was in August 2024, although SITL-POL-010 Section 4 sets an annual external test for a LOW-criticality organisation, and the new financial-services client asks for its summary.

Manila builds its customer portal in-house with its own nine developers. No supplier writes code for the portal or any other Manila system, and there is no contract for development work. Your LI-SOA (T5.2) marks A.8.30 Not applicable, with that justification.
A.8.31 Separation of development, test and production environments

The portal runs in three environments, development, QA and production, each in its own cloud account, under the Manila development lead's own environment rules of 2024, which no other team uses and which have never been reviewed; SITL-POL-012's Group environment standard has not been brought in. Releases reach production only through the pipeline's release job. The nine developers still hold write access to the production database, granted in 2025 for hotfixes and never removed, and they sign in to it with the same accounts they use in development. Nothing is measured.

Changes to the portal follow SITL-POL-009 Section 6.1, the Group change procedure that every office uses and the Group CIO reviews each year: an RFC in the IT service management tool, approved by the weekly Change Advisory Board before the release, with test evidence, a rollback plan and a post-implementation review; an emergency change has its own path. The release engineer checks by hand that an RFC is approved before running the release job; the job itself does not check. Your CHG-TEST (steps 1 and 2) tests 25 of the 64 changes of 1 October to 4 December 2026. Nobody compares the production release log with the approved RFCs. Nothing is measured.

The portal's QA database is refreshed each month with a copy of production, under the portal team's own refresh procedure, written by the Manila development lead in 2025; no other team uses it, and it has never been reviewed: the database administrator raises a request, the Manila development lead approves it, and the request is kept; the QA environment is open to the portal team alone, as production is. The procedure has no masking step, and the Group data-masking procedure (SITL-POL-017), which the CRM test tenant's refreshes follow, is not applied to the portal: end-customers' names, addresses and account numbers are copied as they are, unlike the CRM test tenant's masked copies. An old copy is overwritten at the next refresh, never deleted when testing ends. Nothing is measured.
A.8.34 Protection of information systems during audit testing

Clients' yearly audits include technical tests on Manila's live systems. Each follows the Org CISO's own audit-testing checklist for Manila, approved in 2024; no other office uses it, and it has never been reviewed: the client's test scope and dates are agreed in writing with the Org CISO and the system owner beforehand; testers get read-only accounts, scans run after 20:00 Manila time while the security monitoring team watches, and the accounts are disabled on the day the test ends. The three client audits of 2026 have signed scope letters and account-closure records on file. Nothing is measured.

Tabletop exercise TTX-2026-01 at the Manila office, Tuesday 24 November 2026, played under SITL-POL-014 and the Manila incident response plan. Facilitator: the Incident Response & Crisis Manager (GRC); observer: the Information Security Auditor. A phishing e-mail gives an attacker a team leader's laptop, and a CRM export leaves the office. GlobalConnect holds the export's data for a Manila bank client, as its processor. Every time is in UTC; Manila is UTC+8. Synthetic: written for the exercise.
Facilitator: Incident Response & Crisis Manager (GRC); observer: Information Security Auditor

Before play starts, the facilitator walks the team through the Manila incident response plan. The call tree, replaced in July, still lists a team leader who left in August, and none of the players has rehearsed the plan before.
Call tree corrected before play; each player given a role card; a yearly rehearsal added to the actions

The SIEM alerts on 3.1 GB sent from team-leader laptop MNL-LT-0142 to a personal cloud-storage site. At 02:52 UTC the SOC analyst logs it in the incident tool as INC-2611-0142. Is it an information security incident, and how severe?
SOC analyst, then the Incident Response & Crisis Manager (GRC)
Confirmed as an incident and rated SEV2 on the SITL-POL-014 scale; the Crisis Management Team and the Group CISO told within the hour
An engineer wants to reimage laptop MNL-LT-0142 straight away, to be sure the malware is gone.
Manila IT engineer, with the Incident Response & Crisis Manager (GRC)
The laptop is cut off from the network and left powered on, the cloud-storage site is blocked at the proxy, and the team leader's password and sessions are reset.
Incident response team, with Manila IT
Laptop isolated, site blocked, credentials reset; each action logged in INC-2611-0142

The Privacy Compliance Analyst confirms what the file held: the names, mobile numbers and account numbers of 2,400 customers in the Philippines of the Manila bank client, unencrypted. The DPO must plan the notices to the authority and to the customers, and tell the bank.
Privacy Compliance Analyst, then the DPO

Seven working days later, the post-incident review finds the root cause: the team leader had seen the phishing e-mail the day before and had not reported it, not knowing how. The review proposes actions on the reporting route, on awareness and on the plan.
Root cause and five actions recorded, each with an owner and a date; lessons passed to the risk register and the awareness plan

The product owner writes each feature as a user story. For a story that touches sign-in, payment or customer data, the security acceptance criteria are taken from the Group's application security checklist (SITL-POL-012); the checklist has no card-payment items. The Security Architecture & Standards Manager approves the criteria at sprint planning.
The story, with its security criteria and their approval
Product owner; Security Architecture & Standards Manager
A design change that alters a data flow or an integration is reviewed against the portal team's engineering principles before it is built. A design that fails goes back to the team.

Developers work on branches. Each merge request is reviewed by a second developer against the secure coding essentials (SITL-POL-012 Section 7.1). The build runs a static code scan and a check of the open-source libraries; a High finding stops the build unless the Manila development lead waives it, and the waiver tool has no field for a reason.
Merge request reviews; scan reports; waivers

Each release is deployed to the QA environment. Functional tests run, then the Group security test gate (SITL-POL-012 Section 6.1): a dynamic scan and tests of sign-in and session handling. The product owner signs off acceptance.
Test runs (TR-…) attached to the release ticket; acceptance sign-off

The release's RFC goes to the weekly Change Advisory Board with its test evidence and rollback plan (SITL-POL-009 Section 6.1). Before running the release job, the release engineer checks by hand that the RFC is approved: the job itself does not check.
The RFC and its approval in the IT service management tool
The release job deploys to production on Wednesday at 21:00, Manila time. It is the only deployment path the pipeline has.

Each month the database administrator copies the production portal database into QA, on the Manila development lead's approval of a request under the portal team's own refresh procedure, which has no masking step: end-customers' names, addresses and account numbers are copied as they are, and the old copy is overwritten at the next refresh.
The refresh request and its approval
Within 5 working days of a release, the change owner records in the RFC whether the change worked and caused no incident.
The post-implementation review in the RFC

Development, QA and production each run in a cloud account of their own. The nine developers still hold write access to the production database, granted in 2025 for hotfixes, and sign in to it with their development accounts.
Cloud account and database access lists

F1.2-J1.notice: Sales is answering a client's tender today and has drafted this line: "GlobalConnect's ISMS meets ISO/IEC 27002:2022, the ISO 27000 family standard." I have until noon to approve it or send it back. What do I tell Sales?
options: Approve it: the 27000 standards are one family, so naming 27002 is close enough for a tender
Send it back: the standard to name is ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the one a certificate is issued against, and ISO/IEC 27002:2022 can be described as the guidance behind our controls
Send it back and ask Sales to write "international best practice" instead of a standard's number, so nobody can challenge it

options: Mark all three: she is the compliance lead, and a legal requirement is always an ISMS requirement
Remove the Regulators row from CTX-IP: Legal deals with regulators, so they do not belong in an ISMS register
Keep DOLE labour law compliance out of that column: HR meets it, and the ISMS addresses the requirements about protecting information, such as the NPC registration and the clients' data laws

Yes: write payroll under Exclusions in section 5, since the provider runs it and it is not ours
Yes, once the provider shows its own ISO/IEC 27001 certificate: then payroll can be left out

options: Yes: show Partially met as Met in the board summary and keep the detail in the file
No: Partially met means some of what the clause requires is missing, unapproved or unrecorded (rule L13); show the three statuses as rated, with the biggest gaps first
Show only Fully met and Not met, counting Partially met as Not met, to stay on the safe side

options: Current: his June review counts, and I put a note beside the row

No: only the item that reports active exploitation matters, and the other four are background

That it is not fixed yet: the shared account breaks the Group rule that every person signs in with their own account, so each of the five gets a named account, with an owner and a date, and we report back when the access log shows no shared sign-ins
That it is fixed, once the shared account's password has been changed

T7.2-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

T8.1-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

What do I tell him?
options: The record keeps what the review found: he had seen the e-mail and had not reported it, not knowing how; the actions go to the reporting route and to awareness, each with an owner and a date, and the review does not judge him
Record only that a phishing e-mail reached him: the review should name the attack, not the person

T8.2-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

No: the RTO comes from the business impact analysis and is not changed to fit a test; keep 4 hours in BIA-RTO, record the 9 hours as a gap with a remediation and a retest date, and take any change of the RTO to its owners as a separate decision

T9.1-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

Keep the photo but mark it Good practice: a fire exit has to open for people leaving, and this one is not locked
Keep it: the photo shows a door in the perimeter held open with its alarm isolated, which is a finding on the walkthrough; facilities can own the action, but the finding stays

T9.2-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

options: No: on the test date it is open, past its due date and has no exception in the register, so a booked fix does not cover it; if he wants cover he asks the system owner and the Org CISO for an exception, with a compensating control and an expiry date
Yes: a fix with a date means the owner is acting on it, so the finding is within SLA until the window
Put it in a slower class: the QA server is not customer-facing, so a longer timescale fits and it is not yet late

T10.1-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

options: Yes: once a setting is fixed it is Compliant, and the sheet should show the current state
No: CFG-BASE records the settings as they were at the extract date, 30 November; each fix goes in as an action with an owner and a date, and the setting is checked again after it
Show them as Compliant, with the old value kept in a note so nothing is hidden

T10.2-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

options: Yes: swap them, the sample should show normal practice and he knows which changes were rushed
Draw the whole sample again with a new seed, so that nobody can say the three were picked
No: the draw stands and every change in it is tested as it is; swapping picks for better ones means the sample no longer stands for the whole population, and nobody could repeat it from its seed

T11.1-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

Yes: a count of scans is easy to reproduce, so it is a safer measure than a percentage
Yes on the dashboard, and keep the card's own measure in the LI-KPI file only

T11.2-J1.sim_notice: Training scenario — the people, systems and data in this message are fictional.

Keep one and reword the other as an observation: the Level 2 card is closer to meeting its requirement

Send nothing and log REQ-05 as answered: the auditor will see the 14 January booking in the review pack anyway
