p: COPC CX Standard An industry performance standard for customer-experience operations, written by COPC Inc. Contact centres can be certified against it.
GDPR / DPA 2012 / KVKK Laws. Breach clocks, lawful basis, rights and transfers.
HIPAA A US federal law (1996), enforced by the HHS Office for Civil Rights. Healthcare providers and their business associates must comply.
ISO 9001 A certifiable quality management-system standard: accredited certification bodies audit organisations and certify them against it.

ISO 19011 Guidelines for auditing management systems. An audit finding is the result of evaluating audit evidence against the audit criteria, the requirements audited against. The audit conclusion is the audit team's own, reached from all the findings; the auditee provides the evidence.

ISO/IEC 17021-1 Requirements for the certification bodies that audit and certify management systems, ISO/IEC 27001 among them. A certification body must have a documented process to receive, evaluate and decide on appeals against its decisions (clause 9.7), and one for complaints (clause 9.8).
ISO 18295 A certifiable ISO standard for customer contact centres: service requirements a centre can be certified against.
ISO/IEC 27001 A certifiable management-system standard: clauses 4–10 (Plan-Do-Check-Act) plus 93 Annex A controls.

ISO/IEC 27001 documented information Clause 7.5 controls all of it. Where a clause says the organisation shall “maintain” documented information, it is a document: kept current and changed under control, such as a scope, a policy or a process. Where it says “retain” documented information, as evidence, it is a record: kept unchanged as proof of what was done or found, such as evidence of competence or the results of a review, an audit or a measurement.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 4.1 Understanding the organization and its context. The organisation determines the external and internal issues that are relevant to its purpose and that affect its ability to achieve the intended outcomes of its ISMS. In practice, external issues come from its environment (laws, regulators, technology, markets, threats) and internal ones from within (culture, structure, capabilities). Since Amd 1:2024 it also determines whether climate change is a relevant issue. The issues are used again when the scope is set (Clause 4.3) and when risks and opportunities are planned (Clause 6.1.1).

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 4.2 Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties. The organisation determines a) the interested parties relevant to its ISMS, b) their relevant requirements, and c) which of those requirements will be addressed through the ISMS. An interested party is a person or organisation that can affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by the ISMS, such as customers, employees or a regulator. A requirement is a need or expectation such a party holds; it can be legal, regulatory or contractual. The requirements are used again when the scope is set (Clause 4.3 b) and when risks and opportunities are planned (Clause 6.1.1). Since Amd 1:2024 a note adds that parties can have requirements related to climate change.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 4.3 Determining the scope of the information security management system. The organisation determines the boundaries and applicability of its ISMS to set its scope. In doing so it considers a) the external and internal issues of Clause 4.1, b) the requirements of Clause 4.2, and c) the interfaces and dependencies between the activities it performs itself and those that other organisations perform. The scope is available as documented information. In practice a scope statement names the organisational units, locations, services and technology it covers, and lists the interfaces and dependencies at its boundary. The certification body checks that the scope is credible for the information it claims to protect, and that every exclusion is justified.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 4.4 Information security management system. The organisation establishes, implements, maintains and continually improves an ISMS, including the processes it needs and how they interact (the 2022 edition added the processes and their interactions). In practice each process is written down with the owner who runs it, the inputs it works from and the outputs it hands on, so that one process's output can be followed into the next.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 5.1 Leadership and commitment. Top management shows leadership and commitment to the ISMS by a) making sure the information security policy and objectives are set and fit the organisation's strategic direction; b) building the ISMS's requirements into the organisation's processes; c) making sure the resources the ISMS needs are available; d) communicating why effective information security, and conforming to the ISMS, matter; e) making sure the ISMS achieves its intended outcomes; f) directing and supporting people to contribute to its effectiveness; g) promoting continual improvement; and h) supporting other managers to show leadership in their own areas. In practice the evidence is top management's own acts on record: approvals, budget and resource decisions, minutes, and the communications it issues.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 5.2 Policy. Top management establishes an information security policy that a) is appropriate to the purpose of the organisation; b) includes information security objectives or provides a framework for setting them; c) includes a commitment to satisfy the applicable requirements related to information security; and d) includes a commitment to continual improvement of the ISMS. The policy e) is available as documented information, f) is communicated within the organisation, and g) is available to interested parties, as appropriate. Items a)–d) are about what the policy says; e)–g) about what is done with it.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 5.3 Organizational roles, responsibilities and authorities. Top management makes sure that the responsibilities and authorities for roles relevant to information security are assigned and communicated within the organisation. It assigns the responsibility and authority for a) ensuring that the ISMS conforms to the requirements of ISO/IEC 27001; and b) reporting on the performance of the ISMS to top management. A note adds that top management can also assign responsibilities for reporting on the ISMS's performance within the organisation. In practice the assignments are written down, for example in a RACI and in job descriptions, so that they can be shown to an auditor.

ISO/IEC 27001 A.5.1 Policies for information security (Annex A control 5.1; its guidance is ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Section 5.1). The information security policy and the topic-specific policies are defined, approved by management, published, communicated to the relevant staff and interested parties, who acknowledge them, and reviewed at planned intervals and when significant changes occur. ISO/IEC 27002 Section 5.1 gives example topics for topic-specific policies: access control; physical and environmental security; asset management; information transfer; secure configuration and handling of user endpoint devices; networking security; information security incident management; backup; cryptography and key management; information classification and handling; management of technical vulnerabilities; and secure development.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 6.1.2 Information security risk assessment. The organisation defines and applies a risk assessment process that a) establishes and maintains information security risk criteria, including 1) the risk acceptance criteria and 2) the criteria for performing information security risk assessments; b) ensures that repeated risk assessments produce consistent, valid and comparable results; c) identifies the information security risks: 1) the risks of losing the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information within the scope of the ISMS, and 2) the risk owners; d) analyses the risks: the potential consequences, their realistic likelihood and the resulting levels of risk; and e) evaluates them: compares the results with the risk criteria and prioritises the risks for treatment. It keeps documented information about the process. In practice the criteria of a) are set once, on a method card, so that every assessment uses the same scales. (Summarised in our own words, not the standard's text.)

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 6.1.3 Information security risk treatment. The organisation chooses how to treat each risk and determines the controls that treatment needs, from any source (b). It then compares those controls with Annex A to verify that no necessary control has been omitted (c): Annex A is a list to check against, not a list to adopt whole. It records the result in a Statement of Applicability: the necessary controls, why each is included, whether each is implemented, and why any Annex A control is excluded (d). It formulates a risk treatment plan (e), and obtains the risk owners' approval of the plan and their acceptance of the residual information security risks (f). Notes to the clause add that the organisation can design controls itself or take them from any source, and that the controls in Annex A are not exhaustive: further controls are added where they are needed.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 6.2 Information security objectives and planning to achieve them. The organisation sets information security objectives at relevant functions and levels. They a) are consistent with the information security policy; b) are measurable (if practicable); c) take into account the applicable information security requirements and the results of risk assessment and risk treatment; d) are monitored; e) are communicated; f) are updated as appropriate; and g) are available as documented information, and the organisation retains documented information on the objectives, as a record. When planning how to achieve them, the organisation determines what will be done, what resources will be required, who will be responsible, when it will be completed, and how the results will be evaluated. In practice a measurable objective names what is counted, a target and a date; an activity (buy a tool, run a course) is part of the plan, not the objective.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 7.2 Competence. The organisation a) determines the competence the people doing work under its control need, where that work affects its information security performance; b) makes sure those people are competent, on the basis of appropriate education, training or experience; c) where applicable, takes action to acquire the competence needed, and evaluates whether the action worked; and d) retains appropriate documented information as evidence of competence. A note gives examples of action: training, mentoring or re-assigning current staff, or hiring or contracting competent people.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 7.3 Awareness. People doing work under the organisation's control are aware of a) the information security policy; b) their contribution to the effectiveness of the ISMS, including the benefits of better information security performance; and c) what it means not to conform with the ISMS's requirements. Awareness is what people know and act on, not only a session attended; Annex A control 6.3 is the training that builds it.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 7.4 Communication. The organisation determines the internal and external communications relevant to the ISMS: a) on what to communicate; b) when to communicate; c) with whom to communicate; and d) how to communicate. In practice a communication plan lists each message with these four.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 7.5 Documented information. 7.5.1: the ISMS includes the documented information the standard requires, and what the organisation itself decides it needs for the ISMS to be effective. The ISO management-system standards use two terms for it: documented information to maintain, a document, which says what is to be done or how things stand and is kept current; and documented information to retain, a record, which is evidence of what was done or achieved and is kept unchanged. Where a clause asks for something to be available as documented information, or to be produced, it is a document; where it asks for documented information to be retained, or to be available as evidence of results, it is a record. 7.5.2: when documented information is created or updated, the organisation makes sure of a) its identification and description (for example a title, date, author or reference number); b) its format (for example language, software version, graphics) and media (for example paper, electronic); and c) its review and approval for suitability and adequacy. 7.5.3: it is controlled so that it is available and suitable for use where and when it is needed, and adequately protected (against loss of confidentiality, improper use or loss of integrity): its distribution, access, retrieval and use, storage and preservation (legibility included), control of changes (version control), and retention and disposition. Documented information of external origin that the ISMS needs is identified and controlled too.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 9.1 Monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation. The organisation determines a) what needs to be monitored and measured, including information security processes and controls; b) the methods for monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation, as applicable, to ensure valid results: the methods selected should produce comparable and reproducible results to be considered valid; c) when the monitoring and measuring is performed; d) who monitors and measures; e) when the results are analysed and evaluated; and f) who analyses and evaluates them. Documented information is available as evidence of the results. The organisation evaluates the information security performance and the effectiveness of the ISMS. In practice each measure is written on a measure card that answers a) to f), with its formula, target and threshold, and its results go to the management review (Clause 9.3).

ISO/IEC 27004 Information security management: monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation (ISO/IEC 27004:2016). Guidance for meeting Clause 9.1 of ISO/IEC 27001; it holds no requirements to certify against. It explains what to measure (performance measures, about how well a process or activity is carried out, and effectiveness measures, about how far the ISMS and its controls achieve their intended outcomes), how a measure is built from an information need, with its formula, target and the criteria for deciding what a result means, and how results are analysed and reported. Its annex gives example measures.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 9.3 Management review. Top management reviews the ISMS at planned intervals to ensure its continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness (9.3.1). The review considers (9.3.2): a) the status of actions from previous management reviews; b) changes in external and internal issues relevant to the ISMS; c) changes in the needs and expectations of interested parties relevant to the ISMS; d) feedback on information security performance, including trends in 1) nonconformities and corrective actions, 2) monitoring and measurement results, 3) audit results and 4) the fulfilment of information security objectives; e) feedback from interested parties; f) the results of risk assessment and the status of the risk treatment plan; and g) opportunities for continual improvement. Its results (9.3.3) include decisions related to continual improvement opportunities and any needs for changes to the ISMS, and documented information is available as evidence of them. In practice the inputs are collected into a review pack before the meeting, and the minutes record the decisions.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 10.1 Continual improvement. The organisation continually improves the suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the ISMS. In practice the improvements come from the management review's decisions, from measures that show a trend, and from audits and nonconformities.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 10.2 Nonconformity and corrective action. When a nonconformity occurs, the organisation a) reacts to it: takes action to control and correct it, and deals with the consequences; b) evaluates the need for action to eliminate its causes, so that it does not recur or occur elsewhere, by reviewing it, determining its causes and determining whether similar nonconformities exist or could occur; c) implements any action needed; d) reviews the effectiveness of any corrective action taken; and e) makes changes to the ISMS, if necessary. Corrective actions are appropriate to the effects of the nonconformities met. Documented information is available as evidence of the nature of the nonconformities, the actions taken and the results of any corrective action. In practice an action is closed only when the evidence shows the fix in place and a check that it worked.

ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 9.2 Internal audit. The organisation conducts internal audits at planned intervals to find out whether the ISMS conforms to the organisation's own requirements for it and to ISO/IEC 27001, and whether it is effectively implemented and maintained (9.2.1). It plans, establishes, implements and maintains an audit programme, with the frequency, methods, responsibilities, planning requirements and reporting; the programme takes into consideration the importance of the processes concerned and the results of previous audits (9.2.2). For each audit it a) defines the audit criteria and scope; b) selects auditors and conducts audits so that the audit process is objective and impartial; and c) makes sure the results are reported to relevant management. Documented information is kept as evidence of the programme and the results. In practice auditors do not audit their own work, and ISO 19011 gives the guidance on how audits are run.

ISO/IEC 27001:2022/Amd 1:2024 Climate action changes, published in February 2024. It adds one sentence to Clause 4.1: the organisation shall determine whether climate change is a relevant issue. It adds a note to Clause 4.2: relevant interested parties can have requirements related to climate change. Nothing else changes: the clauses are still 4 to 10 and Annex A still has its 93 controls.
NIST CSF 2.0 A voluntary framework: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

PCI DSS A card-data security standard set by the PCI Security Standards Council, founded by the card brands; not a law, and not contract wording itself: contracts with banks and card brands require merchants and service providers to meet it. No certificate is issued to the organisation: compliance is shown by a qualified assessor's Report on Compliance on their controls.

r: Copy the first five parties listed in the table of addendum Section 4 (Stakeholder requirements), in the same order, with the requirement written next to each.

Walk the SITL-STD-001 Section 5 decision tree from Q1. Then apply SITL-POL-004 Section 3.1: personal data, children's data and credentials are never below Tier 3; aggregated data takes the highest tier of its parts, and at least the tier of what the parts show when read together; derived outputs take the tier of the source.
Write: "Because of <cause>, <event> may occur, leading to <consequence> for <asset>." Copy the words for cause, event and consequence from the scenario facts. Copy the asset name from the register.

Find the likelihood and impact descriptor in the ERM scale table (SITL-ERM-001 Section 6.2–6.4) that uses the same words as the facts. Write the descriptor number. Residual likelihood = inherent likelihood − 1 for each existing control marked "working" (lowest value 1). Residual impact = inherent impact. Score = likelihood × impact. Rating: 1–5 Low, 6–11 Medium, 12–19 High, 20–25 Critical.
LOW-criticality appetite = 11. Residual score ≤ 11 → Decision "Accept and monitor". Residual score > 11 → Decision "Treat"; due days from SITL-ERM-001 Section 7: Critical 30, High 90, Medium 180.
If a sentence has two actions (joined by "and" or ";"), make two rows. Owner role = the owner of the linked SITL policy in the SITL-POL-000 index.

Look up the control frequency in Ref-Sampling and copy the minimum sample. Where what you sample is a population of records (the accounts of one review), use its population-of-records row. The platform draws the sample at random once your sample size is checked.

Effective: no exceptions. Effective with exceptions: only Low/Medium exceptions and ≤ 5 % of the population. Not effective: any High exception or > 5 %. Control tests (T8.2): 1–2 deviations = effective with exceptions; > 2 = not effective.
One change-log row for each changed field: row ID, field, old value, new value, event ID, evidence.

Class 1: on an internet-facing asset, KEV-listed or Critical → 7 days. Class 2: on an internal asset, Critical or KEV-listed → 14 days. Class 3: High → 30 days. Class 4: Medium → 90 days. Due = first detected + SLA. Exception valid only if approved by system owner AND CISO, has a compensating control, and has not expired.
High = affects a Mission Critical system or no evidence exists. Medium = done late or partly. Low = record-keeping only.

Use the tier from rule R35. Then include every question in Ref-Questions marked for that tier or a lower tier. Clause checklist: include every clause marked for the tier; add "transfer mechanism" if data leaves the country.

Role = decided by who decides why and how the personal data is processed (SITL-POL-017 Section 3.2). DPIA required = Yes if the activity involves any of: children or students, AI/analytics/profiling, monitoring or recording, health data, identity checks (KYC/AML). Otherwise No. This is the Group's screening rule: GDPR Art.35 asks for a DPIA wherever processing is likely to result in a high risk, so an activity outside this list can still need one.

For every affected office and every data-subject country, look up the regimes in addendum Section 2. Deadline = discovery time (UTC) + clock. Mark the earliest firm deadline. Tell data subjects = Yes if the data includes children's data, health data, financial data or credentials, or more than 1,000 people; otherwise No. This is the Group's screening rule: GDPR Art.34 itself asks, case by case, whether the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the people concerned. Exception (GDPR Art.34(3)(a)): No if the data was unreadable to whoever took it, for example encrypted with a key they do not have. The clocks are the controller's: where the organisation holds the data as a client's processor, it also tells that client without undue delay (GDPR Art.33(2)), early enough for the client to meet the deadline you marked.

Use the 4-week template: Week 1 lesson, Week 2 poster + quiz, Week 3 phishing simulation, Week 4 results + refresher. Copy the scenario card and the 3 behaviours for your theme from Ref-Content. Approvals: HR + Legal always; add works council where addendum Section 2 lists one for the office.

Answer each request with ONE evidence file: the record the auditor asks for (not a plan, a template or a policy where a record is asked for), under the same clause or control, for this office, dated inside the audit period, from a system or a controlled document (not an undated screenshot). Record its file ID and SHA-256. If no file holds what is asked, answer "No evidence available" and raise an action, with an owner and a date, to produce it from now on: never create evidence after the request.

Critical: access to Tier 4 data or children's data at scale, OR a customer-facing or regulatory-critical service that is hard to replace. High: access to Tier 3 personal/confidential data at volume, OR a revenue-critical service. Medium: limited personal data or pseudonymous data, easy to replace. Low: only public/anonymous data. Check from Critical down; stop at the first match.

Low → Risk owner. Medium → Org CRCO. High → Org CEO + Group CISO. Critical → Not acceptable (Board decision). Source: Charter Section 6.1. Always use this table, even if the register shows a different value.

Decide each document's type from what it is for and who uses it. Requirements standard (certifiable): it sets the requirements an organisation's management system shall meet, and an accredited certification body can certify the organisation against it. Requirements for certification and audit bodies: it sets the requirements a body that audits and certifies management systems shall meet, not requirements for the organisations it certifies. Guidance standard: it gives guidance or guidelines (on controls, implementation, risk, measurement or auditing) and holds no requirements to certify against. Vocabulary: it gives the overview and the terms and definitions the family uses.

Place each clause of ISO/IEC 27001 by what it does in the cycle. Plan: establishing the ISMS — understanding where it operates, who leads it, what it must achieve and what it needs. Do: operating the ISMS as planned. Check: monitoring, measuring, auditing and reviewing it. Act: correcting and improving it.

Write the ISMS scope (Clause 4.3) for the office in hand, one line per part, each with the source it was read in: the organisational units, the location, the services and the technology it covers; the interested parties' requirements the ISMS addresses (CTX-IP); each exclusion with its justification, or None; and the interfaces and dependencies with activities other organisations perform, each with the Annex A control that governs it.

List the ten ISMS processes (Clause 4.4), each with its owner, inputs and outputs. The owner is the role that runs the process: read it where Ref-ISMS processes (Learn › Reference pages) says, for most processes the role marked R on its row of the GRC Charter Section 16 RACI (the role abbreviations are spelled out under the table). The inputs are what the process works from; the outputs are what it hands on.

A control is Applicable when a risk, a legal or contractual requirement, or a business need calls for it, and Not applicable only when the office does nothing the control governs: record that justification, and review it if that changes. Every Annex A control stays in the SoA. For an applicable control, record the source that calls for it, read in its facts: Risk, where a risk in the risk register or in your risk treatment plan (LI-RTP) is treated with it; Legal requirement, where a law or a regulator's rule requires it; Contractual requirement, where a client or supplier contract requires it (PCI DSS reaches Manila through its card-handling clients' contracts); Business need, where the Group requires it of every office or the office needs it to run. Where the facts give more than one, record the first in that order. A control is still applicable when only part of the office does what it governs.

Implemented? in the SoA: for a control already sprinted, its status in your tracker T-LI-CIT (column D), with its evidence ref (column F); for a control whose sprint is still to come, Planned, with its sprint and week; for an excluded control, Not applicable. The platform carries them over from the tracker and the plan.

Check the information security policy against Clause 5.2 a)–g), one item at a time. Found only when you can cite the section of the policy that meets the item: the section whose own words say it. Where a statement points on to another section (a procedure, the document control), cite the statement. What an office reports doing counts only where the policy or its record shows it. Gap: no section meets the item, and its section is None.

Read each certification fact on Ref-Certification card (Learn › Reference pages), the summary of ISO/IEC 17021-1 and ISO/IEC 27006-1: what each audit stage reviews, how nonconformities are graded and closed, who decides, and how long the certificate lasts and how it is kept. Brief management in the card's terms, not from memory.

Choose one option for each risk (ISO/IEC 27005:2022), from its residual score and the facts of the risk. Ask in order and stop at the first Yes. 1) Is the residual score within the appetite (SITL-ERM-001 Section 4: 11 for a LOW-criticality organisation)? Yes → Retain (accept): keep it as it is, monitor it, and raise an acceptance request (SITL-POL-002 Section 6.2). 2) Can the activity that causes the risk be stopped, or not started, without losing what the office needs it for? Yes → Avoid. 3) Can controls the office runs bring the likelihood or the impact down? Yes → Modify (reduce). 4) Otherwise → Share: another party, an insurer or a supplier under contract, carries part of the consequence. A Critical risk (20–25) is never retained (SITL-ERM-001 Section 7).

Rate each requirement from what was found, held against what the clause requires. Fully met: everything the clause requires is in place at the office, with the evidence it asks for (approved documents, records). Partially met: some of it is in place, or it is in place but not approved, not done everywhere it should be, or without its records. Not met: none of it is in place.

Set each objective (Clause 6.2) consistent with the information security policy (SITL-POL-001 Section 3.1: measurable, set each year, tracked), measurable where practicable (what is counted, a target and a date), and from the results of the risk assessment and treatment and last year's results (SITL-POL-001 Section 6.2). For each, record what will be done, what resources will be required, who will be responsible (the role R for its process, GRC Charter Section 16), when it will be completed and how the results will be evaluated (the measure, who measures it and how often).

Break each objective's plan into at least two milestones, each with what is delivered and its date, the last on or before the objective's own date. Progress against them is measured each quarter on the objectives dashboard (SITL-POL-001 Section 6.2, step 3).

Major = the required activity was never done in the period OR failed in more than half of the sample. Minor = any other failure. This is the Group's working test: ISO/IEC 17021-1 calls a nonconformity major when it affects the management system's ability to achieve its intended results.
Copy the service model from the vendor intake form. Copy the responsibility table for that model from the sheet Ref-Cloud. Add the 5 fixed cloud and supply-chain questions from the same sheet.

Phases: plan (A.5.24), detect and report, assess and decide (A.5.25), respond (A.5.26), learn (A.5.27); evidence A.5.28. Invoke the DR plan if a Mission Critical system is unavailable longer than its RTO. Invoke the BC plan if a critical process has stopped longer than its RTO. Otherwise "Do not invoke".

Year 1: clauses 4–10 + Annex A organisational; Year 2: people + physical; Year 3: technological. Auditor = Internal Audit (never the process owner). Frequency: controls with open or repeat actions in T12.1 are audited every year.

Fill one row per Clause 9.3.2 input (a to g, with d in its four parts). Available: a file of the pack holds it; name that file as the source. An input about changes is available only where the file records a review that looked for changes. Missing: no file holds it, and its source is None. Opportunities for continual improvement are ways to make the ISMS better beyond fixing what failed; a line that answers a measure in the red is feedback on performance. Stage 1 readiness (the Group's working test): Yes only when an internal audit of the ISMS has been held and reported (rule L23's first year: clauses 4–10) and a management review has met with every input; otherwise No, with what must happen first. Corrective actions still open do not by themselves stop Stage 1, as long as each is tracked to closure.

Open the evidence the finding names and read what it shows. Where it supports the finding, accept it and respond in three parts (Clause 10.2), each with an owner and a date: the correction, which fixes this nonconformity now; the root cause, why the process let it happen (a cause in the process, not a person's name); and the corrective action, which changes the process so that it does not happen again. Dispute a finding only with evidence that the requirement was met: at the closing meeting, then through the certification body's appeal process.

F1.1: What will I do
Onboarding to the ISMS implementation programme. Complete onboarding: record your assignment, sign the undertaking and data rules, and submit your completed Onboarding record file.
Why am I doing this

Every GRC (Governance, Risk and Compliance) job starts with conduct: you handle other people's data and you produce records that auditors rely on. Before you touch any task, the organisation needs proof that you know the rules (SITL-POL-024 Section 6.1) and that your workspace records your work correctly.
What will I learn
Follow the mentee conduct and data rules — synthetic data only, own work, no AI tools for task work — see SITL-POL-024 Section 3.1; SITL-POL-022 Section 7.1
Recognise what a controlled record looks like: hash, UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) time, version, naming convention — see Capture standard — SITL-MEN-101 Section 9
Use the scripted help: the help note (?) on every step, the glossary and the "Report a problem" form — see Guided Model — principle G7
Keep task data only in your platform folders (00_Admin, 01_Inputs, 02_Working, 03_Submission) — see SITL-STD-001 Section 6 — row "Mentee use"; Capture standard — folders
How to do it

6 numbered steps, of which 3 are decisions from options (judgement share 50 %). Rules you will use: copy and calculation only (Learn › Rule tables). Assigned by the Cybersecurity Program Manager, who has written the help note (?) on every step. Help is pre-written on the platform (no live chat).
What to read or refer
SITL-POL-024 — Section 3.1 policy statements; Section 6.1 Procedure: Mentee onboarding
SITL-POL-005 — Acceptable Use Policy
SITL-POL-022 — Section 7.1 Guideline: Using generative AI safely (no AI tool is used for task work)
SITL-STD-001 — Section 6 Handling matrix — row "Mentee use"
SITL Group GRC Charter — Section 10 and Section 10.1 Rules of engagement for mentees
Reference pages (Learn › Reference): Ref-Rules
Where to add

Platform: Home › My Organisation, My Tasks, My plan; F1.1 step 3 (onboarding attestations). Template: Platform forms (ADM-UND, ADM-RULES) and the file Onboarding record (ONB-RMF) (issued in /M2610-00001/W01/F1.1/01_Inputs). Submit to /M2610-00001/W01/F1.1/03_Submission. GRC record: Admin folder /M2610-00001/00_Admin.
What to deliver
ADM-UND — Signed undertaking (Platform e-signature)
ADM-RULES — Data rules acknowledgement (Platform check-boxes)
ONB-RMF — Completed Onboarding record file (DOCX (file Onboarding record, three fixed tables))
DEC-LOG — Decision log (Platform (automatic))
Why is this important

Without a signed undertaking your account is not opened for data (SITL-POL-024 Section 6.1 step 3). A confirmed conduct breach later is an automatic fail (SITL-MEN-101 Section 13.2 gates). The manifest you test here is the same mechanism that makes every later submission auditable. Feeds: every task (ADM-RULES).

principles: G1
Half instructions, half decisions
About 50 % of every task's activities are decisions made from options provided; the rest are numbered instruction steps. Each task shows its judgement share.
G2
Decisions use provided options
The mentee never writes an opinion from nothing: each decision offers fixed options (A/B/C, or a drop-down per row). The rules in Ref-Rules tell the mentee how to choose.
G3
Feedback after every decision
After submission the mentee sees the best option and a one-line reason. Wrong choices are learning points, not penalties beyond the scoring weight.
G4
Fixed templates and sentence frames
Outputs are templates with drop-down lists. Where text is needed, the mentee completes a sentence frame. Free writing is not assessed.
G5
Plain English
Short sentences, common words, one action per step (CEFR level B1). A glossary explains every GRC term. English style is never scored.
G9
Foundation weeks: less is more

Weeks 1–2 teach one rule per task with a worked example before every decision type: no risk assessment, no Lead Implementer extension, at most six steps and three decisions per task, at most eight hours per week, one scripted message per task.
G6
Task messages carry a learning point

Each task sends scripted messages (one in the Foundation weeks, two from week 3): a situation to decide (A/B/C) and either an extra data file or a data-handling decision. Each ends with why it matters.
G7
Help is scripted, never a chat

There is no agent or person to chat with. Every step carries a pre-written help note (?) and names its rule; the Learn section holds the glossary and the rule tables; "Report a problem" is a form answered by the programme office. Nothing on the platform gives the answer to a decision.
G8
Reviews check decisions and evidence
Reviews check decisions and evidence: the automatic check scores decision accuracy against the key, correct rule application, evidence for every row, and data handling.

The 12-Week Plan shows the planned task hours per week (about 6–8 hours in weeks 1–2, 12–16 hours from week 3). Only due dates and submitted work are checked.
Reminders and scripted task messages arrive in the platform inbox and stay there until the mentee opens them; nothing is sent outside the platform.
If the mentee records no activity for 7 calendar days, the programme office makes a welfare check.

items: Weekly knowledge checks: 10 questions, 15 minutes, open book, two attempts (new form each time).
Foundation Gate Exam at the end of week 2: 30 questions, 45 minutes, pass mark 70 % (one resit).
Performance tasks: the extracts you receive contain planted problems. The rules find them when you apply them step by step.
Decisions: about half of every task; scored against the answer key (best option per situation or per row).
Task messages: one per task in weeks 1–2, two per task from week 3; a situation to decide and an extra data file or data-handling decision.
Final Exam in week 12: 40 questions (60 min) plus a 30-minute practical — a 60-row access extract with 8 hidden exceptions.
gates: All 25 tasks submitted, every step complete (each step is checked against its key before it can be marked complete).
Foundation Gate Exam passed at 70 % or more (one resit on a new form within 5 working days).
Final Exam passed at 60 % or more (including the practical station).
No confirmed integrity breach (use of live/real data, copying another mentee's work, impersonation, or use of any AI tool for task work: the platform has no chat assistant; all help is scripted).
acrit: All required artefacts, fields and rows present; every numbered step ticked in the work log.
Accuracy and decisions against the answer key
Decision points: best option chosen (per scenario, per row for item decisions). Planted defects found, no false findings, calculations correct within tolerance.
Every finding has an evidence reference (row ID or clause); references are real and correctly cited.
Template unchanged, naming convention, manifest, steps ticked and rule IDs recorded.
Submitted by the system due date; task messages answered within 2 working days.
hcrit: Choices match the key; where a choice differs, the rule and evidence cited show a reasonable reading. Patterns of wrong choices become coaching points.
Every value has a source (document + section, or dataset row) in the "Evidence ref" column.
Instruction steps done; rules applied as written; templates and frames used as issued; task messages answered.
Accuracy and completeness of the record
Values copied exactly; calculations correct; no empty required field.
Only workspace data used; drills reported; own work; nothing sent outside the platform.
bands: and no composite below 75; digital badge "GRC 101 — Distinction"
remediation path: repeat up to 4 failed weeks in the next cohort with newly generated, unique tasks (once)
levels: Would be accepted by an experienced practitioner without change; shows insight beyond the brief.
Meets the brief fully; minor issues only.
Mostly meets the brief; some material errors or gaps that a reviewer would send back.
Partially meets the brief; significant errors; needs close supervision.
Missing, wrong, or not the mentee's own work.
hc: Rules R04 and R05 applied correctly; facts copied accurately with a source for every value; decision-tree path recorded for every asset.

Rules R11–R13 applied correctly; look-ups complete; redlines follow the frame; fix location (Group or Addendum) correct. ISO/IEC 27001 LI extensions: LI-05 — L06/L07 applied exactly; every justification has a source. LI-06 — L08/L09 applied exactly.
Rules R09, R15 and R18–R20 applied correctly; test plan followed unchanged; every exception traceable to a dataset row.

Rules R06–R08, R19, R22 and R24–R26 applied correctly; numbers traceable; test script followed unchanged. ISO/IEC 27001 LI extensions: LI-09 — L12 applied correctly. LI-11 — L16 applied; formula reproduces the value. LI-12 — L17/L18 applied exactly.
Rules R28 and R30 applied correctly; every deadline traceable to an addendum row; legal sign-off box ticked. ISO/IEC 27001 LI extensions: LI-14 — L20 applied correctly.

Rules R33 and R34 applied correctly; closure decisions and escalations justified by the evidence; right evidence file for each auditor request; response to the finding follows the evidence. ISO/IEC 27001 LI extensions: LI-17 — L23/L24 applied correctly; readiness verdict follows the rule. LI-18 — clause quoted; response follows the evidence.
inject_format: Situation — one or two short sentences from the current task (plain English).
Options — A, B, C (DECISION and DRILL), or numbered steps for an extra data file (DATA).
Learning point — shown after answering: the best option and why it matters.
Read — the rule or document that guides the choice.
inject_rubric: DECISION/DRILL: best option chosen. DATA: rows added and rules applied correctly.
DECISION: a defensible but weaker option (named in the key). DATA: rows added with one error.
Answered late (after 2 working days) or DATA incomplete.
Not answered, wrong option, OR (DRILL) the offered data was accepted or forwarded.

human: Cybersecurity Program Manager (policy owner of SITL-POL-024) or delegate.
Runs monthly calibration, AI-reviewer assurance sampling, final re-checks and cohort reporting.
voice: every pre-written note gives one instruction at a time in simple English, says which rule applies and where the value is, and never gives the answer to a decision

stages: Know the organisation, its laws and standards, its policies and who decides what.
Know the assets, classify them, find the risks and rate them against the appetite.
Map requirements to controls, manage suppliers, protect personal data, train people.
Collect good evidence, test controls and access, answer the auditor.
Track every finding to closure, report to management, respond to change.
T12.1 (and every finding you raise in weeks 3–11)
threads: Who the organisation is, which laws and standards apply, and what changes when a regulator changes the rules.
What the organisation owns, how sensitive it is, what can go wrong and how much risk management will accept.
How a legal or contractual requirement becomes a control, a policy statement and a step someone follows.
How you prove a control works: good evidence, a fair test, a clear exception, an action that really closes.
Risk that comes from outside: suppliers, their reports, the personal data they and we process, and what to do when it leaks.
Your own conduct and data rules, how staff learn safe behaviour, and how the ISMS talks to its people.

programme.audience: Fresh graduates and career-changers with no GRC experience; English may be a second language
programme.model: Guided Execution Model: about half of each task is numbered instructions and half is decisions made from provided options, guided by rule tables, with feedback after every decision
